title: Sally Goodin
alternative_titles: Sally Gooden
description:
'Sally Goodin' has a claim to being the first commercial country music recording in history. On June 30 and July 1, 1922, Texas fiddler Eck Robertson (1887–1975) and Henry Gilliland traveled to Victor Records in New York City — legend has it they showed up uninvited after performing at a Confederate Veterans' reunion in Richmond — and recorded several sides. Robertson's solo recording of 'Sallie Gooden' on July 1 was released by Victor later that year, predating the Fiddlin' John Carson and Vernon Dalhart recordings often cited as country music's commercial beginnings. 'Sally Goodin' itself is a Texas contest fiddle showcase, built around a simple base melody that expands into a cascading series of variations. The tune was a competitive vehicle — Robertson used it to demonstrate his technique, particularly his facility in the high register and his command of string crossings — and it became the standard by which Texas-style contest fiddling was measured. Ralph Peer, who would later record the Carter Family and Jimmie Rodgers, supervised the session. The name may refer to a real woman in Robertson's community or simply be a rhyme-placeholder common in folk naming.

A field recording of this tune by Henry Reed was made for the Library of Congress in 1966 (American Folklife Center).

notes: This is a showpiece — start with the base melody and then learn at least three or four variations before performing it. The base melody sits in A major and is deceptively simple; the variations climb into the high register and demand confident bow technique. Texas contest style: the bow arm drives from the elbow, the tone stays full even at high speed, and variations should flow seamlessly from one to the next without a break. Don't rush — Eck Robertson played it with absolute authority, not with panic. Listen to the 1922 Victor recording if you can; it's the original template.

title: Fire on the Mountain
alternative_titles: Run, Moses, Run
description: One of the most-played tunes in all of American old-time music, 'Fire on the Mountain' appears in American fiddle collections from the late 19th century and was almost certainly in oral circulation for decades before that. The image of fire on the mountain — visible across vast distances in the days before electric light, signaling danger or celebration — was a powerful metaphor in a culture where the mountains themselves defined the horizon. Early recordings by mountain string bands in the 1920s and 30s cemented its place as a session anchor. The pentatonic structure in A major makes it nearly impossible to play a wrong note on an in-tune fiddle, which is why it's among the first tunes beginners learn — but its rhythmic drive and forward momentum reward advanced players who discover what they can do inside those simple bones. Bill Monroe, Flatt and Scruggs, and Tommy Jarrell all recorded versions, each bringing a distinct interpretation to the same elemental melody.

Advanced players: experiment with double-stops in the A part for more fullness. The B part calls for the bow to move higher on the string; don't let the energy drop there. At a fast jam tempo, 'Fire on the Mountain' becomes an endurance test and a joy. Play it until it plays you.

title: Old Joe Clark
alternative_titles: Joe Clark
description: Named for a real person — Joseph Clark, born September 18, 1839, in Clay County, Kentucky — 'Old Joe Clark' is one of the most universally known tunes in the Appalachian tradition. Clark served in the 7th Kentucky Infantry (Union) during the Civil War, discharged in 1862 due to disability, and returned to the eastern Kentucky mountains where his name became attached to a body of floating comic and satirical verses. The tune itself is almost certainly older than the man, adapted from earlier dance music and given Clark's name when the local community found the verses irresistible. By the early 20th century it had spread across the mountains, collected in multiple states with dozens of verse variants. Cecil Sharp gathered versions in the 1910s. 'Old Joe Clark had a yellow cat / She would neither sing nor pray / She stuck her head in the buttermilk jar / And washed her sins away' is among the most memorable. The tune crossed into bluegrass and remains one of the first tunes any beginner learns. Bill Monroe, Doc Watson, and countless others recorded it. Its A major setting — simple, driving, pentatonic — is nearly universally playable and singable.

The Mixolydian variant (with G natural instead of G sharp) has a modal bite some players prefer. The B part lifts into a higher register and then comes back down — play the contrast clearly. For banjo players, this is a canonical clawhammer tune. For fiddlers, it's a workout in bow economy and rhythm. Sing a verse: 'Round and round, Old Joe Clark / Round and round I say / Round and round, Old Joe Clark / I ain't got long to stay.'

title: Shady Grove
alternative_titles: She Is Shady Grove
description: One of the most haunting tunes in the Appalachian repertoire, 'Shady Grove' was first published in the Journal of American Folklore in 1915 but almost certainly predates that collection by decades. The melody shares deep DNA with the English ballad 'Matty Groves' (documented as early as 1613) and surfaces in an American manuscript as far back as 1786 in 'Henry Beck's Flute Book' — making it one of the oldest documented folk melodies on American soil. The tune's emotional grip comes from its Dorian mode: E Dorian in most American versions creates a feeling that hovers between major and minor, never fully landing in either, which gives 'Shady Grove' its characteristically bittersweet longing. The text follows the floating-verse tradition of Appalachian song: the 'shady grove' is a place of meeting, courtship, and loss — specific enough to feel real, vague enough to hold every listener's version. Jean Ritchie's recordings brought it to the folk revival. Doc Watson, Clarence Ashley, and the Grateful Dead all recorded it, cementing its status as one of the few Appalachian tunes with genuine crossover life.

In sessions it works beautifully played once slowly, then repeated as an instrumental. The B part has a yearning quality that resolves without fully resolving — lean into that ambiguity.

title: Cripple Creek
alternative_titles: Going Up Cripple Creek
description: Often the first tune a beginner fiddler learns, 'Cripple Creek' runs deeper than its reputation as a starter tune suggests. Named for Cripple Creek in Wythe County, Virginia — a real stream, not the Colorado gold rush town — the tune has been in continuous oral circulation since at least the late 1800s, with a documented reference in the Journal of American Folklore in 1915 and a version collected by Cecil Sharp in 1917 from Kentucky singers. Fiddlin' John Carson recorded it in 1923 in one of the earliest documented old-time recordings. The tune belongs to the broader family of creek and river songs — 'Going Down to Cripple Creek, going in a run / Going down to Cripple Creek to have a little fun' — where the creek is a place of escape, courtship, and release from daily labor. Its A-major setting and pentatonic skeleton make it one of the most accessible tunes in the tradition while its rhythmic drive keeps it compelling at any tempo. Bill Monroe, Earl Scruggs, and Don Reno all recorded it, carrying it deep into the bluegrass canon.

At speed, the string crossings in the B part are the technical challenge. Don't let its beginner reputation make you underplay it — a well-driven 'Cripple Creek' at full tempo is serious music.

title: Blackberry Blossom
description:
Popularized in the 1920s and 30s but likely older in origin. 'Blackberry Blossom' belongs to the category of 'decorated' tunes — its flowing melody invites ornamentation in a way that simpler breakdowns do not. The tune crossed from Old-Time into early bluegrass, becoming a vehicle for virtuosic picking. Flatt & Scruggs and later Doc Watson helped cement its place in American acoustic music.

The recording heard here is by Jeffrey Wood & Trevor Wood, preserved by the Internet Archive.

title: Whiskey Before Breakfast
alternative_titles: The Scottsman, Spirits In The Morning, Whiskey 'Fore Breakfast, Whiskey For Breakfast, Whisky Before Breakfast
description: Despite its lighthearted title, 'Whiskey Before Breakfast' is a tune of real melodic beauty. Its origins are obscure — it appears in neither O'Neill's nor most early American collections — suggesting it may be a 20th-century composition that achieved the status of a traditional tune through widespread adoption. It has become a jam session standard across Old-Time and Celtic traditions, valued for its singable melody and clean structure.

In Celtic sessions this is played with more lift; in Old-Time sessions it's smoother.

title: Arkansas Traveler
alternative_titles: Arkansas Traveller, Arkansaw Traveler, I'm Bringing Home A Baby Bumblebee
description:
The 'Arkansas Traveler' comes with one of the most specific and entertaining origin stories in American folk music. Around 1840, Colonel Sandford C. 'Sandy' Faulkner (1803–1874), a Kentucky-born cotton planter and Arkansas politician, got lost while campaigning through the Ozark back country. He stopped at a log cabin and found the settler initially unhelpful — until Faulkner, an accomplished fiddler, recognized the tune the man was struggling with and completed the second part of it. The settler instantly transformed from surly stranger to gracious host. The story became a comic dialogue about Yankee vs. Southern manners, city vs. country, traveler vs. local — and the tune became its soundtrack. Albert Fay published the tune and its dialogue sketch in 1847; it was one of the first pieces of music to be attributed to a specific Arkansas source. By the Civil War, 'Arkansas Traveler' was known across America. Thomas Hart Benton painted the famous scene in 1959. The tune has been recorded by more artists than can be counted and remains one of the most recognized American folk melodies in the world.

A field recording of this tune by Henry Reed was made for the Library of Congress in 1967 (American Folklife Center).

notes: The A part is the 'lost traveler' half — incomplete and searching. The B part is the 'completion' that the settler couldn't find — confident, conclusive, and funny to play after the A part hangs unresolved. This is a showpiece tune: learn both parts and practice stopping dramatically after the A to let the pause land. At fiddle contests, it's traditional to play it up-tempo with elaborate variations. At jams, keep it simple and emphasize the call-and-response quality.

title: Soldier's Joy
alternative_titles: Billy Peddle, Chicken In The Bread Tray, The Clap Dance, Da Soldiers Joy, French Four, The Gower, The King's Head, Lumbers
description:
Documented in print as early as 1780 in Thompson's 'Compleat Collection,' Soldier's Joy may derive from an English country dance called 'The King's Head.' Laudanum (opium) was once nicknamed 'soldier's joy,' lending the tune a darker folk etymology. It spread across the American South through the 18th-century fiddle tradition and remains the most commonly played tune at Old-Time jam sessions worldwide.

A field recording of this tune by Henry Reed was made for the Library of Congress in 1967 (American Folklife Center).

title: Kitchen Girl
alternative_titles: Kitchen Gal, The Kitchen Girls
description: A reel of uncertain origin that has circulated in Appalachian and Celtic traditions, 'Kitchen Girl' evokes the social world of early 20th-century rural households where music was made in the kitchen during informal gatherings. The domestic setting — the kitchen as the social heart of the home — was a common site for music-making in pre-radio Appalachian communities. The tune was collected in multiple versions across the Southern mountains.

title: John Henry
description: John Henry's story — a Black steel-driver who raced a steam drill through a Virginia mountain and won, then died with his hammer in his hand — is one of the central myths of American industrial labor. The historical event probably occurred at the Lewis Tunnel on the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway in Summers County, West Virginia, around 1870–1872. Whether a real John Henry died there is disputed; what is indisputable is that the song and the myth spread through the railroad gangs of the late 19th century with the speed of fire. By the 1920s it had been collected across the South in hundreds of versions. The fiddle tune version captures the relentless hammering rhythm of the original work song in A minor — the driving downbeats, the unrelenting forward motion, the sense of a man working against a force that will outlast him. Guy Johnson's 1929 book 'John Henry: Tracking Down a Negro Legend' was the first scholarly treatment.
notes: Feel the hammer in your bow arm. The A minor key and relentless rhythm should convey effort and power — this is not an easy or gentle tune. The steady quarter-note feel in the A part should sound like hammer blows. The B part provides rhythmic contrast. At medium-fast tempo, the tune acquires the inexorable quality of work that cannot stop. Don't rush; real hammer work has a steady, sustainable rhythm. Emphasize the downbeats.

title: Angeline the Baker
alternative_titles: Angelina Baker
description:
Stephen Foster published 'Angelina Baker' in 1850 for the Christy Minstrels, writing it at a moment of intense national debate over the Fugitive Slave Act and the expansion of slavery. The original was a sentimental song in minstrel dialect about an enslaved woman separated from her lover by sale — a subject Foster returned to repeatedly, using the conventions of minstrel performance to express what the historical record suggests was genuine grief about the institution of slavery. The fiddle tune adapted from Foster's melody stripped the lyrics and transformed the song into a dance tune, a common fate for Foster compositions that spread virally through 19th-century America. By the Civil War era, 'Angeline the Baker' was circulating as an instrumental far removed from the Christy Minstrels stage. By the time it reached the 20th-century old-time revival, it had accumulated over 50 years of folk transmission and dozens of regional variants. It appears in numerous early fiddle recordings and remains a standard in both old-time and bluegrass sessions.

The recording heard here is by Tom Joad, preserved by the Internet Archive.

Good for beginners because the structure is clear and the melody is singable. Pairs well with other D-major tunes in a set.

title: Sandy River Belle
description:
One of the cornerstone tunes of the Round Peak style and the Tommy Jarrell repertoire, 'Sandy River Belle' takes its name from the Sandy River, which flows through Surry and Forsyth Counties in North Carolina — the heart of the musical region that Jarrell, Fred Cockerham, and their contemporaries called home. Tommy Jarrell (1901–1985) played with a bow arm power and directness that defined Round Peak fiddle for generations of revival players who came to study with him in the 1970s; 'Sandy River Belle' exemplifies that style at its most characteristic. The tune's A major setting and two-part structure are conventional; what's unconventional is the way Jarrell's bowing — heavy, close to the bridge, with deliberate drone-string use — transforms a simple melody into a full-body rhythmic experience. It was recorded by Jarrell and documented in the Field Recorders' Collective archive.

The recording heard here is by Tom Joad, preserved by the Internet Archive.
tags: tommy jarrell, surry county, north carolina, round peak
notes: Learn the Round Peak approach before you attempt this tune: bow close to the bridge, use the full length of the bow, let the lower strings drone. Tommy Jarrell's recordings are the mandatory reference — listen until you understand not just the notes but the bow weight and the rhythmic feel. The A part drives forward; the B part has a slight lift. Don't clean it up; the roughness and directness are the music, not defects to be corrected.

title: Cold Frosty Morning
description:
A signature tune of the Round Peak, North Carolina tradition, 'Cold Frosty Morning' was recorded by the Da Costa Woltz Southern Broadcasters in 1927 — one of the earliest Old-Time commercial recordings. Tommy Jarrell (1901–1985), son of fiddler Ben Jarrell, kept this tune alive for generations through his influence at the annual Fiddler's Grove festivals in Union Grove, NC.

The recording heard here is by Big Foot Lane, preserved by the Internet Archive.
tags: tommy jarrell, jam session, G major
notes: Tommy Jarrell learned this from his father Ben Jarrell, who recorded it in 1927. The G major setting sits comfortably in first position — great for beginners but with enough melodic interest to keep advanced players engaged. Play the A part firmly, then let the B part lift slightly. The tune pairs naturally with a banjo in clawhammer style.
audio_source: Big Foot Lane via Internet Archive

title: St. Anne's Reel
description:
One of the most widely-played reels in North America, 'St. Anne's Reel' is a point of convergence between Old-Time, Celtic, and Quebec fiddle traditions. Its exact origins are disputed — claimed by both Irish and French-Canadian traditions. It was recorded in the early 20th century by Canadian fiddlers and adopted into Old-Time through the shared dance hall culture of the 19th century.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by Bob Hill and his Canadian Country Boys, digitized by the Internet Archive.
notes: A deceptively simple tune that rewards clean, even bow strokes. Practice the string crossings in the B part slowly — they can blur at speed if not drilled. This tune crosses genre lines freely: play it in an Old-Time jam, a Celtic session, or a Quebec contradance and you'll fit right in. In Old-Time style, flatten the rhythm slightly; in Celtic style, lift it more.
audio_source: Bob Hill and his Canadian Country Boys via Internet Archive
audio_attribution: Bob Hill and his Canadian Country Boys

title: Rye Whiskey
description: A song of whiskey culture from the Appalachian tradition, 'Rye Whiskey' belongs to a broad category of drinking songs that blend humor with genuine pathos. Rye whiskey — distilled from rye grain — was the dominant spirit of the American frontier, produced in home stills throughout Appalachia. The song's modal tonality gives the comedy a darker undertow. It was collected by John Lomax, Cecil Sharp, and multiple folklorists across the Southern mountains.
notes: A song-tune with a wry, world-weary humor — 'Rye whiskey, rye whiskey, rye whiskey I cry / If I don't get rye whiskey I surely will die.' Play it with that resigned, philosophical quality. The modal scale gives it a haunted quality that goes beyond simple comedy. Many fiddlers play it slowly and deliberately, almost like a lament.

title: Cluck Old Hen
description: One of the most peculiarly titled tunes in old-time music, 'Cluck Old Hen' was first transcribed as early as 1886 and recorded most influentially by Fiddlin' John Carson in 1923 — one of the earliest commercial old-time recordings. The tune belongs to the Mixolydian/Dorian modal family that characterizes a large swath of Appalachian music: A Dorian or A Mixolydian depending on the version, with a G natural where a major scale would place a G sharp. The lyrics follow the hen as a rural metaphor: 'My old hen's a good old hen / She lays eggs for the railroad men / Sometimes one and sometimes two / Sometimes enough for the whole damn crew.' The railroad workers, the hen, the counting of eggs — this is the texture of mountain rural life in the late 19th century before electrification, when the railroad was the most powerful external force in every mountain community. Charlie Bowman's version in DGdg tuning and Joe Birchfield's version are among the essential reference recordings. It has been widely played and adapted across Appalachian, bluegrass, and folk revival contexts.
notes: The Mixolydian mode (G natural in an A context) is the tune's soul — if you accidentally play G sharp you lose everything. The melody sits low in the hand, mostly first position, with open-string drones that ring naturally. The lyrical rhythm should drive the bow: 'MY old HEN's a GOOD old HEN' gives you the accent pattern. Try playing it in A Dorian for a darker, bluesier feel that some versions favor. The tune responds well to heavy bow pressure for dancing.

title: Bonaparte's Retreat
alternative_titles: Bonaparte's Defeat, The Retreat Set Dance, The Retreat
description:
Named for Napoleon's catastrophic 1812 retreat from Moscow — one of the great military disasters of the 19th century — 'Bonaparte's Retreat' is believed to derive from an older Irish march called 'The Eagle's Whistle' or 'The O'Donovan Clan March.' The tune reached America with Scots-Irish immigrants and was thoroughly naturalized into the Southern fiddle tradition, collecting regional variations from Virginia through Kentucky and Tennessee. The Kentucky version, in A major, became the most widely known through its adoption into the square dance and contradance circuit. Carl Sandburg included a version in 'The American Songbag' (1927), cementing its status as a legitimate American folk artifact. Bill Monroe recorded a definitive version, and it became a standard in the early bluegrass repertoire. The tune's powerful A-part drive and its floating, almost wistful B-part mirror the arc of Napoleon's campaign: confident advance, then disintegration. Bill Harrell's recording and the many versions in the Appalachian fiddle contest tradition are the benchmark references.

A field recording of this tune by Henry Reed was made for the Library of Congress in 1966 (American Folklife Center).

Published as early as 1788 in the New York Magazine, 'Liberty' is one of the oldest distinctly American fiddle tunes. Its name reflects the post-Revolutionary spirit, though the tune itself may have older British roots. It became a contest staple across the South and Midwest. Variations abound — some fiddle communities play it in D, others in G.

A field recording of this tune by Henry Reed was made for the Library of Congress in 1966 (American Folklife Center).

notes: A tune with enormous rhythmic drive — feel the pulse in your bow arm, not just your fingers. The A part has an ascending run that should build energy. Don't rush; keep a solid floor tempo and let the notes speak. The B part contrast is crucial: the jump up to high position should feel like a release of pressure. Doc Watson and many North Carolina fiddlers favored this one.

title: Black Mountain Rag
description: Doc Watson's arrangement of 'Black Mountain Rag' transformed what was already a well-known piece into one of the defining showpieces of modern old-time and folk guitar. Watson (1923–2012) of Deep Gap, Watauga County, North Carolina, developed his flatpicking technique in relative obscurity before the Newport Folk Festival in 1960 brought him to national attention; 'Black Mountain Rag' became his signature. The tune itself derives from 'Stone's Rag,' a Texas-style fiddle piece by Sidney Stone, which Watson adapted for guitar with dazzling speed and clarity. Black Mountain is a real place — a community in Yancey County, North Carolina — lending the tune its Appalachian identity even as the guitar arrangement drew from the Texas instrumental tradition. For fiddle players, the tune offers a different challenge than for guitarists: the speed and the clean string crossings required to match Watson's clarity at tempo.
notes: This tune is a technical showpiece and should be treated as one. Learn it slowly — the fingering in the B part is treacherous at speed. Doc Watson's recordings are the gold standard; study his phrasing and note choices closely. The A part has a rolling quality; the B part has a leaping, more angular character. Keep the bow close to the bridge for brightness. Don't add ornaments you haven't practiced — at the tempos this tune is usually played, unplanned flourishes become train wrecks.

title: Waterbound
description:
In pre-bridge Appalachia, being 'waterbound' — stranded by a flooded creek or river — was a frequent and sometimes dangerous predicament that could last days. Mountain roads followed creek beds and crossed streams repeatedly, making heavy rains an instant barrier. The tune captures the patient waiting of someone stuck on the far bank, watching the water rise and fall. It was widely collected across the Blue Ridge and Smokies.

The recording heard here is by Derek Piotr, Guy Wolff, preserved by the Internet Archive.
notes: A song-tune where the 'waterbound' refers to being stranded on the wrong side of a flooded creek — a common predicament in pre-bridge Appalachia. Play it with patient, philosophical energy; being waterbound meant waiting. The melody is gentle and flowing — let the phrases breathe. This is a tune that sounds beautiful played slowly at medium volume.
audio_source: Derek Piotr, Guy Wolff via Internet Archive (2023)

title: Wildwood Flower
description: Originally published in 1860 as 'I'll Twine 'Mid the Ringlets' by Maud Irving and Joseph Philbrick Webster, the song was transformed by the Carter Family's 1928 Victor recording into the most recognizable guitar piece in American folk music. Sara Carter's rhythm guitar and Maybelle Carter's melody-lead style became the template for country guitar. A.P. Carter adapted the lyrics. The tune's journey from parlor song to country classic exemplifies the Carter Family's role in defining American vernacular music.
tags: carter family, parlor song, singable, history
notes: The fiddle version flows naturally in C major — let the melody sing. This was originally a parlor song ('I'll Twine 'Mid the Ringlets'), and that parlor sensibility should come through: refined, gentle, lyrical. The Carter Family's guitar accompaniment defined the tune's character, but the fiddle version can carry that same dignified quality. Don't rush; let each phrase settle.
audio_source: Johnny Cash & June Carter via Internet Archive

title: Chinquapin Hunting
description: The chinquapin (Castanea pumila) is a small native chestnut tree that once grew throughout the Appalachian understory, its sweet nuts harvested by both Native Americans and Appalachian settlers in autumn. Chinquapin hunting — gathering the small, sweet nuts after the first frost — was a beloved seasonal activity for Appalachian children and families. The American chestnut blight (1900–1940) killed billions of trees, including the chinquapin; many communities lost a food source that had fed them for generations. The tune carries an elegiac undertone for a lost landscape.
notes: A light, playful tune — the chinquapin hunt was a children's activity, and the music should have that carefree quality. Keep the bow arm relaxed and the rhythm bouncy. Don't over-articulate; let phrases run together naturally. Works beautifully at a moderate tempo where dancers can actually feel the groove.

title: Fly Around My Pretty Little Miss
alternative_titles: Fly Around
description:
A song-and-dance tune from the Appalachian tradition, 'Fly Around My Pretty Little Miss' is a courtship song with roots in English and Scots-Irish balladry. The simple verse structure and dancing rhythm made it a social function staple in mountain communities. Collected in multiple versions across Virginia, North Carolina, and Kentucky, it represents the song-tune category — music that exists equally as song and instrumental piece.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by Samantha Bumgarner, digitized by the Internet Archive.
notes: A song-tune, meaning the melody follows natural speech rhythm. Sing the words in your head as you play: 'Fly around, my pretty little miss / Fly around, my daisy.' This will help you phrase naturally rather than mechanically. Great for beginners because the form is clear and predictable. Pair it with a banjo for maximum Old-Time effect.

title: Sugar in the Gourd
description: Sugar in the gourd was literally sweet sorghum or cane sugar stored in a dried hollow gourd — a common practice in 19th-century Appalachian households before commercial packaging. Sorghum molasses was one of the few sweeteners available to mountain families. The tune, with its pentatonic leanings and driving rhythm, was collected across multiple Southern states and represents the category of 'household item' tunes that filled the Old-Time repertoire.
notes: A pentatonic-leaning breakdown with a rhythmic hook that hooks listeners immediately. The 'gourd' is a dried hollow gourd used as a water dipper or storage vessel — a staple of 19th-century rural households. Keep the bow arm driving and let the open strings ring. The rhythm has a slight syncopation that's easy to feel once you've found the groove.

title: Wolves A-Howlin
description: Wolves were a genuine presence in Appalachian mountain life well into the 19th century, preying on livestock and occasionally threatening communities. 'Wolves A-Howlin' evokes the frontier soundscape of early settlement — the wild, unpredictable darkness beyond the cabin window. The tune was collected in the Round Peak tradition of Surry County, North Carolina, and is associated with Tommy Jarrell's modal repertoire. The last wolves in Virginia were extirpated around 1900.
tags: tommy jarrell, round peak, modal, howling
notes: One of the most evocative titles in the Old-Time canon — play it like you're hearing wolves in the dark. The modal quality (often Dorian or pentatonic) gives it a genuinely unsettling undertone. Keep the bow slow and heavy in the slower sections. Tommy Jarrell's version is the definitive reference. Don't try to brighten this up — the darkness is the point.

title: Blackest Crow
description: 'Blackest Crow' belongs to the haunted interior of the Appalachian song tradition — a D minor modal song and tune whose lyric confronts the duration of love against the entropy of nature. 'As long as this world will last / I'll love you till the rivers run dry / The blackest crow that ever flew will surely turn to white.' The inversion of natural expectation — the crow turning white, the rivers running dry — defines love as something that will outlast the impossible. The melody is as stark as the lyric: narrow in range, slow in movement, with the kind of simplicity that makes it immediately memorable and devastatingly effective. Multiple versions exist across Virginia, West Virginia, and North Carolina, where it was collected in the early 20th century. Iris DeMent and Tim O'Brien recorded a widely heard version in the folk revival; the tune has also been recorded as a purely instrumental piece.
tags: haunting, minor, D minor, mountain, slow
notes: This is a slow song-tune — don't confuse it with a reel or breakdown. The melody should move at the pace of speech, breathing naturally through each phrase. D minor with a modal quality (watch the 6th and 7th degrees for inflection). Let the longing of the lyric shape your bow arm: long, sustained notes with expressive bow pressure changes. If you learn the words, they'll tell you how to play it. This tune should leave silence in its wake.

title: June Apple
alternative_titles: The June Apple, June Apples, The June Apples
description:
Named for a variety of apple that ripens in early summer in the Southern Appalachians, 'June Apple' is a Mixolydian reel with roots in the mountain fiddle tradition. The Mixolydian mode — associated with Scots-Irish modal music — gives it a slightly archaic quality that distinguishes it from major-key dance tunes. It has been collected in multiple versions across Virginia, North Carolina, and Kentucky.

The recording heard here is by Derek Piotr, Guy Wolff, preserved by the Internet Archive.

The tune has an irresistible forward momentum — find the groove and stay in it. The B part provides a rhythmic contrast that feels like release. Many players add a slight lilt on the second eighth note of each beat pair for a more authentic Old-Time feel.
audio_source: Derek Piotr, Guy Wolff via Internet Archive (2025)

title: Leather Britches
description: 'Leather Britches' has one of the most appetizing titles in the old-time repertoire. 'Leather britches' are string beans dried in their pods — a preservation technique widespread across the Appalachian mountains before refrigeration, where the beans were strung on thread and hung to dry in kitchens and porches through late summer, then cooked with fatback through winter. The drying process turns them leathery and chewy, intensifying their flavor. The fiddle tune carrying this name appears in American collections from the 18th century and is almost certainly older still, sharing melodic material with British dance tunes of the same era. It was a ballroom and court dance tune in its earlier life; in the mountains it became a driving reel. Flatpicker Doc Watson recorded an influential version, and it remains one of the most commonly played tunes at Appalachian jams.
tags: ancient, appalachian, G major, folk history
notes: G major with a driving, confident quality that suits its history as a ballroom tune transformed into mountain music. The two parts have distinct characters — A is more rhythmically propulsive, B has a longer melodic line. Doc Watson's flatpicking version gives guitarists a model; fiddle players should match that energy with bow arm weight. The title is a conversation starter: tell the story of dried beans to anyone who asks what 'leather britches' means.

title: New Ground
description: In Southern Appalachian culture, 'new ground' referred to freshly cleared land — forest converted to farmland through the labor-intensive process of felling trees, pulling stumps, and breaking sod. This was one of the defining agricultural experiences of frontier settlement. Tunes named for agricultural activities — 'New Ground,' 'Plowing Under,' 'Harvest Home' — reflect the centrality of farming to rural Southern life and the music that accompanied it.
notes: 'New ground' was the Southern term for land just cleared of trees for the first time — ready for planting. Play this with the energy of clearing that ground: forceful, purposeful, rhythmically driven. The G major setting and open-string drones give it a full, outdoor sound. A natural jam session opener because the form is clear and the rhythm is irresistible.

title: Hickory Jack
description:
Hickory (Carya spp.) was one of the most valued trees in the Appalachian forest — hard, shock-resistant, and used for tool handles, wagon wheels, axles, and furniture. The name 'Jack' was a generic working-class name in American folk culture (see also 'Cracker Jack,' 'Flapjack,' 'Steeplejack'). Hickory Jack as a character represents the competent, self-reliant Appalachian worker — the backbone of the mountain economy. The tune has a similar character: reliable, sturdy, unpretentious.

The recording heard here is by Boyd Asher, preserved by the Internet Archive.
notes: A solid, workmanlike breakdown — 'Hickory Jack' sounds like a character you'd want clearing timber. Play it with honest, grounded energy: no flashy tricks, just clean notes and steady rhythm. The hickory wood reference suggests hardness and durability — bring that quality to the bow arm. Great for session contexts where you want something dependable.

title: Ducks on the Millpond
description: 'Ducks on the Millpond' evokes one of the most pastoral images in Appalachian folk life: the millpond, built to power a grist mill, where the community's grain was ground and where, inevitably, a few ducks would settle on the still water. The millpond was a social hub in mountain communities — a place where neighbors met while waiting for their corn to be ground — and naming a tune for it situates the music in a specific, deeply local world. The tune itself has a gentle, unhurried quality in A major that differs from the driving breakdowns more typical of old-time music, giving it a slightly contemplative character. It was played both as a dance tune and as a piece of pure musical pleasure. The two-part AABB structure is symmetrical and singable.
notes: Let the tune breathe — it's not meant to be driven hard. The A major key with open-string drones gives it a ringing, open quality. Imagine the millpond: still, flat, reflective. The bow should move smoothly rather than driving aggressively. Good for slowing down a jam session or transitioning between faster reels. Play it with the unhurried confidence of someone who isn't in a hurry to get anywhere.

title: Shaking Down the Acorns
description: Mast — the nuts of forest trees including acorns, hickory nuts, beechnuts, and chestnuts — was a critical food source in Appalachian agriculture. Pigs were turned into the forest in autumn to fatten on mast, a practice called pannage or 'masting.' Shaking acorns from low branches and collecting fallen mast was seasonal labor that involved whole families. The tune captures the energetic, festive quality of this autumn harvest activity.
tags: tommy jarrell, round peak, autumn, energetic
notes: A lively, physical tune with a harvest-season energy. Shaking acorns from oak trees was a genuine activity — gathering mast for pigs, making flour, or just for the pleasure of the noise. Keep the rhythm driving and the bow arm active. The tune has a slightly 'falling' quality that reflects the acorns coming down.

title: Granny Does Your Dog Bite
description: A nonsense song-and-dance tune from the Appalachian comic tradition, 'Granny Does Your Dog Bite' belongs to the category of humorous call-and-response pieces that were performed at square dances and play parties. Grandmother figures in Appalachian folk culture were simultaneously respected and gently satirized — their dogs (usually fierce guard dogs on mountain homesteads) were respected too. The tune's light humor reflects the social function of dance music as community entertainment.
notes: A comic question-and-answer song-tune — play it with a grin. The rhythm has a playful hitch to it; don't smooth it out. The humor in the title should come through in the music. Great for children and beginners but satisfying for experienced players who add slurs and ornaments on the repeats.

title: Cricket on the Hearth
description: Named for the beloved hearth cricket of Appalachian mountain homes. The delicate, light bow style needed to render the crickets' chirps makes this a bow technique challenge.
notes: Use a light, fast bow close to the tip — aim for a crisp, chirping sound.

title: Brimstone
description: Brimstone — sulfur — was the scent of hellfire in the fire-and-brimstone preaching tradition of Appalachian evangelical Protestantism. The term appears dozens of times in the King James Bible, always associated with divine wrath and eternal punishment. The tune's dark modal character reflects the theological atmosphere of the Great Awakening revivals and the camp meeting tradition that swept Appalachia from the 1790s onward. Music and religion were inseparable in mountain culture.
notes: A dark, modal tune that earns its hellfire name — brimstone (sulfur) was the smell of hell and damnation in traditional Protestant theology. Don't play this bright or fast; let the modal quality and the darkness develop. A slow-to-medium tempo reveals the menacing character. Let the open strings drone and sustain freely.

title: Log Cabin Blues
description: The log cabin was the defining architectural form of American frontier settlement — built quickly from available timber, warm in winter, intimate in scale. By the early 20th century, the log cabin had become a symbol of hardy American individualism, romanticized in popular culture even as actual log cabins were being replaced by milled-lumber houses. The 'blues' suffix places the tune in the 1920s–1930s commercial folk era when 'blues' attached to traditional tunes signaled a progressive, modern sensibility.
notes: A modal blues tune that lives in a minor-tinged, open-fifth sound world. Don't rush toward the resolution; let the modal ambiguity sit. The log cabin setting suggests isolation, self-sufficiency, and the weight of frontier life. Play it slowly enough that the modal character registers. Good string crossings and clean open-string drones are essential.

title: Nine Hundred Miles
description:
A railroad song of uncertain origin that has been collected across multiple American traditions — Appalachian, blues, and labor song. The '900 miles' represents the crushing psychological distance from home experienced by itinerant workers, railroad laborers, and migrants. The Carter Family recorded it; Woody Guthrie recorded it; it appears in Lomax collections. Its wide distribution suggests it was a genuine folk song that traveled with the workers who sang it.

The recording heard here is by Pete Seeger, preserved by the Internet Archive.
notes: A song-tune about a railroad journey — 'If my woman quits me, Lord, I'm 900 miles from home.' The modal quality gives it genuine pathos. Play slowly and with feeling; don't rush. The melody should feel like the endless monotony of distance. Woody Guthrie and the Carter Family both recorded versions. This is a tune that rewards simplicity over technique.

title: Chinquapin
description: The chinquapin (Castanea pumila) — a small chestnut native to the Appalachian understory — is now rare following the chestnut blight that began in 1900. In earlier centuries it was a food staple, medicine source, and seasonal landmark. This modal tune, distinct from 'Chinquapin Hunting,' uses a minor-pentatonic scale that predates European diatonic harmony — suggesting origins in either very old Scots-Irish tradition or Native American musical contact zones of the Southern Appalachians.
notes: A dark, modal tune — the minor pentatonic scale gives it a haunted, ancient quality. Play slowly and let the open strings drone freely. Don't rush toward the resolution; let the modal ambiguity breathe. Many players find this tune meditative at slow tempos. The chinquapin nut — small, sweet, now mostly gone — gives it an elegiac quality.

title: Bonaparte Crossing the Rhine
description: Napoleon Bonaparte crossed the Rhine River multiple times during his campaigns (1796, 1805, 1813), transforming European political geography. His Rhine crossings were major news events that captured the imagination of ordinary people across the Western world. American fiddle tunes named for Napoleon — 'Bonaparte,' 'Bonaparte's Retreat,' 'Bonaparte Crossing the Rhine' — reflect the intense popular fascination with the French Emperor, who was simultaneously admired for his military genius and feared as a tyrant.
notes: A fast, bright reel with heroic overtones — Napoleon crossing the Rhine was a major historical event, and the tune has that grand, sweeping quality. Keep the bow arm confident and forward. The A part marches; the B part dances. A strong tune for large sessions where you need something with momentum.

title: Old Bunch of Keys
description: A quirky Appalachian reel with a cascading melody that sounds like keys jangling. The unusual title matches the tune's unpredictable character.

title: Hook and Line
description:
A D major reel with a fishing theme — the elegant, darting phrases suggest a line cast into a mountain stream.

The recording heard here is by George "Shortbuckle" Roark, preserved by the Internet Archive.
audio_source: Roark, George Shortbuckle" via Internet Archive (1938)

title: Stoney Creek
description: Stoney Creek is a community in Patrick County, Virginia, in the Blue Ridge foothills near the North Carolina border — one of the richest areas for Old-Time fiddle tradition. The region, associated with the fiddle and banjo style known as Round Peak, produced legendary players including Tommy Jarrell, Fred Cockerham, and Kyle Creed. Water features — creeks, rivers, fords, and springs — were the central landmarks of Appalachian geography, and dozens of tunes carry their names.
tags: henry reed, LOC recording, virginia, grayson county
notes: A cool, clear reel that sounds like the water it's named for. Let the bow float through the phrases with a light, liquid touch. The A part flows downward; the B part rises. Stoney Creek tunes tend to be associated with the Round Peak and Galax regions — play it with that flat-footed, grounded rhythm underneath the flowing melody.

title: Rose Tree
description:
An 18th-century English and Irish dance tune, 'Rose Tree' (also 'The Rose Tree') appears in multiple period collections including Playford's Dancing Master tradition. It was one of the tunes that crossed the Atlantic in the early settlement period, carried by British immigrants. The rose was one of the most culturally significant flowers of the European tradition — symbol of love, beauty, and brevity of life. The tune's graceful character reflects its origins in formal social dancing contexts.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by Frank Fallon and His Orchestra, digitized by the Internet Archive.
notes: A courtly, 18th-century melody with a formal dignity — this tune came from a world of minuets and country dances, not barn dances. Play it with a poised, upright posture in the bow arm and clean, articulate notes. The melodic line has a floral, ornamental quality; let the phrases breathe and complete themselves fully.
audio_source: Frank Fallon and His Orchestra via Internet Archive

title: Lynchburg Town
description: A Virginia reel associated with Lynchburg — a center of trade and culture in the Appalachian mountain region.
tags: virginia, lynchburg, trade town, D major

title: Beaumont Rag
description:
'Beaumont Rag' is among the defining pieces of Texas Western swing and contest fiddle, named for the industrial port city of Beaumont in southeast Texas — oil country, on the Louisiana border, where Cajun and Southern influences merged in a culture distinctly Texan. Bob Wills (1905–1975) and his Texas Playboys popularized the tune and recorded it in the late 1930s; Wills was himself a committed fiddler before becoming primarily a bandleader, and his instrumental recordings document the transformation of old-time fiddle into Western swing. The 'rag' designation signals the syncopation that separates Texas breakdown style from straight old-time: the bow arm must swing, not march. The tune circulates widely at Texas and Southwestern fiddle contests and appears in the repertoires of virtually all serious contest players.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by The Woodshed Four, digitized by the Internet Archive.
tags: texas swing, bob wills, rag, jazz influence
notes: The syncopation is everything — if you play it straight, you lose the entire point. The bow arm must swing: feel the off-beats, put slight emphasis on the second and fourth eighth notes of each beat pair. Texas style calls for a warm, full tone even at speed; don't let the bow pressure lighten when the tempo rises. The B part has a long, looping melodic line that contrasts with the more rhythmic A part. Listen to Bob Wills's 1930s recordings and study how his fiddlers handled the groove.
audio_source: THE WOODSHED FOUR via Internet Archive

title: Salt Creek
description: A reel in the Old-Time tradition that was adopted into early bluegrass by Bill Monroe and popularized through his recordings. 'Salt Creek' — named for a tributary of the White River in Indiana — represents the crossover moment when Old-Time fiddle material entered the nascent bluegrass vocabulary. The tune's popularity on both sides of the genre divide makes it a useful bridge for musicians crossing between communities.

Clean left-hand articulation is key.

title: Grey Eagle
description: An A major breakdown with deep Texas contest fiddle roots, 'Grey Eagle' appears in early fiddle contest records from the 1880s and was collected by Marion Thede in her 1967 compendium 'The Fiddle Book.' The eagle — symbol of American independence — gave the tune its proud, bright character. It was a showpiece for demonstrating high-position technique and clean string crossings at Southern fiddling contests.

notes: The high E-string licks in the B part are the signature of this tune — hit them cleanly and let them ring. Texas players often add a quick slide up into the first note of the phrase. Keep the A part grounded with strong downbows, then lift for the B part. This tune rewards confident playing; timid bowing makes it sound thin.

title: Dusty Miller
description:
A tune of Scottish and Irish origin, 'Dusty Miller' references the miller whose clothes were perpetually covered in flour dust — a stock figure in British folk humor and song. Published in multiple early collections including Gow's 'Repository of the Dance Music of Scotland' (1799), it crossed the Atlantic and appeared in American fiddle books throughout the 19th century. The name was applied to various tunes across traditions, suggesting it functioned as a generic 'miller's tune.'

The recording heard here is by Jock Tamson's Bairns, preserved by the Internet Archive.
notes: An old tune with a courtly feel — don't rush it. The dotted rhythms in some versions suggest a mild hornpipe influence. The A part has a satisfying arc that should feel inevitable; the B part offers contrast. In Scottish tradition this is played with more ornamentation; in Old-Time settings it's typically stripped down and driven forward.
audio_source: Jock Tamson's Bairns via Internet Archive (2000)

title: Over the Waterfall
description:
A reel of unclear origin that has circulated widely across Old-Time, Cajun, and Celtic traditions. Its neutral melodic character — pleasant but not highly distinctive — may explain its adaptability across styles. It has been published in both American fiddle collections and Irish music compendia. The name evokes a natural image that fits the smooth, flowing melody.

The recording heard here is by R. Dunne, preserved by the Internet Archive.

The D major setting means all four open strings are available as drones. Great for practicing smooth string crossings. In Cajun settings, this tune gets a very different treatment — slicker and more ornamental.

title: Brilliancy
description: 'Brilliancy' is a demanding Texas contest fiddle piece whose name announces its purpose: this is music designed to dazzle. Contest fiddling in the South and Southwest developed a distinct performance culture in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, with competitors expected to showcase technical facility — high-position playing, rapid string crossings, ornamental variations — alongside musical taste. 'Brilliancy' belongs to this category of purposeful showpieces, where the melody is a vehicle for demonstrating what a fiddler can do. The tune appears in Texas fiddle contest culture by the early 20th century and was circulated by contest veterans who passed it to younger players as a teaching piece for advanced technique.
notes: The name is a challenge. 'Brilliancy' expects you to be brilliant — clear tone, clean articulation, high-position comfort, and confident tempo. Learn it slowly and build speed only after every note is clean. The high-register passages are the technical core: bow pressure must stay consistent even as the bow works near the tip. Contest players usually learn multiple variations; if you know only the base melody, it doesn't yet dazzle. Keep working.

title: Bob Wills Breakdown
description: Bob Wills (1905–1975), the 'King of Western Swing,' was born in Limestone County, Texas into a deep fiddle family. His father and grandfather were both contest fiddlers. Wills merged Old-Time Texas fiddle with jazz harmonies, jazz horns, and a dancehall groove to create Western swing in the 1930s. His band, the Texas Playboys, recorded prolifically for Columbia and Vocalion. Bob Wills was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1968.
tags: bob wills, western swing, jazz, dancehall
notes: This tune captures the essence of Western swing — a groove that floats between Old-Time fiddle drive and jazz swing feel. Don't play it dead straight; let the bow breathe slightly on the offbeats. Bob Wills' rhythm was infectious — he drove his band from the back of the stage, hollering encouragement while playing. Find that same looseness.

title: Lee Highway Blues
description:
US Route 11 — designated 'Lee Highway' after Confederate General Robert E. Lee — was one of the first numbered US highways (1926), running from Washington DC through the Shenandoah Valley and down through Tennessee and Alabama. It was a major route before Interstate 81 supplanted it. The highway blues tradition reflects Depression-era experience of migration, displacement, and the search for work along American roads.

The recording heard here is by Doc Watson, Clint Howard, and Fred Price, preserved by the Internet Archive.
tags: bob wills, blues, swing, texas playboys
notes: A tune with a 1930s highway feel — somewhere between a breakdown and a blues. The 'blues' quality comes from the bent notes and slight drag on certain beats. Don't play it too clean; let some rawness through. US Route 11 (Lee Highway) cuts through Virginia and Tennessee — play this like you're driving it late at night.
audio_source: Doc Watson, Clint Howard, and Fred Price via Internet Archive (1966)
audio_attribution: Doc Watson, Clint Howard, and Fred Price

title: Faded Love
description: 'Faded Love' was written by Bob Wills (1905–1975) and his father, John Tompkins Wills, who had played an older fiddle tune that Bob adapted into the version recorded by the Texas Playboys in 1950. The song's lyric — about a love that has faded like the roses in the rain — became one of the great country love songs, recorded by Patsy Cline in 1963 in a version that reached millions of listeners who had never heard of Bob Wills. The melody has a quality rare in fiddle music: it's equally effective as an instrumental, a slow country ballad, and a dance waltz, because the tune itself carries emotional weight that doesn't depend on lyrics. The chord progression moves through the circle of fifths in a way that sounds both inevitable and surprising, giving trained musicians something to admire alongside the accessible beauty that non-musicians simply feel.
tags: bob wills, western swing, waltz, patsy cline, country classic
notes: A waltz in G major, played slowly and with feeling. The bow arm should be relaxed and the tone warm — this is not the place for a bright, driving stroke. The melody rises and falls in long arcs; follow those arcs with your bow and don't interrupt them for ornament. Patsy Cline's 1963 recording is the vocal benchmark. For instrumental versions, listen to the Texas Playboys original. The final phrase should leave the room quiet for a moment.

title: Dallas Rag
description: Dallas, Texas was a major center of commercial country and western music recording in the 1920s and 1930s. Labels including Columbia, Victor, and OKeh regularly staged recording sessions in Dallas to capture the rich musical culture of the Southwest — from Western swing to gospel to string band music. 'Dallas Rag' evokes this era of commercial folk recording when the city was a crossroads of African American, white Southern, and Mexican musical traditions.
notes: A 1920s ragtime-inflected tune with syncopation that should feel natural, not forced. The 'rag' quality comes from the rhythmic displacement — lean into the off-beats. This sits in the same sonic territory as 'Peacock Rag' and 'Dallas Rag' recordings from the early commercial era. Let the bow arm swing slightly.

title: Midnight on the Water
description:
'Midnight on the Water' is widely attributed to Luke Thomasson and/or Charles Cunningham of Bosque County, Texas, and is one of the most hauntingly beautiful tunes in the American fiddle tradition. The D minor waltz has a quality of still, dark water — which is precisely what the title evokes — and in the right hands can stop a crowded dance hall. Texas fiddler Benny Thomasson (Luke's son) made it a centerpiece of his contest performances, and the tune spread through the contest circuit into wider circulation. It belongs to a category of Texas fiddle waltzes — along with 'Over the Waterfall' and 'Over the Waves' — that function more as slow, expressive performance pieces than as functional dance accompaniment. The three-part structure (AABBCC) gives it more room to develop than a standard two-part tune.

The recording heard here is by Jack Saturday, preserved by the Internet Archive.
notes: Play this alone, in the dark, for someone you love. D minor with a plaintive, singing melody that asks for a long, slow bow and maximum tone. Don't rush any phrase — this is one of the few fiddle tunes where slowing down only improves it. The high point of the C part should be the emotional peak of the performance; build toward it in the A and B parts. Benny Thomasson's recordings are the essential reference. This is the tune that makes non-musicians understand what a fiddle can do.

title: Yellow Rose of Texas
description: 'The Yellow Rose of Texas' was first published in 1853, attributed to 'J.K.,' and is believed to reference Emily D. West, a free Black woman from New York who may have distracted General Santa Anna during the Battle of San Jacinto in 1836. The tune became Texas's unofficial anthem and was a Civil War marching song for Confederate troops. Mitch Miller's 1955 recording sold over a million copies, cementing its place in American popular memory.
notes: Play it bright and forward — this is a marching tune at heart. The bow should feel light and lifted, not heavy and pressed. The simple four-bar structure repeats enough to allow variation: add slides on the repeats, or ornament the long notes. Great for building a steady, reliable tempo. Audiences always recognize it, which gives you confidence.

title: Peacock Rag
description: The ragtime influence on Old-Time fiddling was substantial in the 1920s — Scott Joplin's rags (1899–1917) had permeated popular culture, and fiddle players absorbed the syncopated rhythms into their repertoire. 'Peacock Rag' belongs to a category of rag-influenced dance tunes that appeared in Southern and Midwestern fiddle contests of the 1920s, reflecting the era's appetite for modern, syncopated music. The peacock's flamboyant display suggested the showmanship required.
notes: A 1920s rag-influenced tune with a strut to it — a peacock spreads its tail to show off, and you should bring some of that pride to the playing. The syncopation should feel natural and hip, not mechanical. This is a tune where tone quality matters: a full, warm sound in the upper strings makes the showoff quality land.
audio_source: D.D.Teoli Jr. A.C. via Internet Archive

title: Texas Gales
description: A Texas reel with a rushing, wind-swept quality. The wide intervallic leaps and fast bow strokes suggest the open prairie in a strong wind.

'Rakes' — young men who lived for pleasure and dissipation — were stock characters of 18th-century Irish folk humor. The tune settled into New England contradance tradition and remains a staple of sessions on both sides of the Atlantic.

title: Money Musk
description:
'Money Musk' is one of the oldest and most historically documented reels in the New England and American fiddle tradition. It appears in print as early as 1788 in William Vickers's Scottish dance book, under the name 'My Lord Musk's Reel' — Lord Musk being a Scottish nobleman whose estate name lent the tune its label before American corruption turned it into 'Money Musk.' The tune crossed the Atlantic with Scots-Irish and English immigrants and became foundational in New England contradance music; it appears in virtually every early American dance manual and fiddle collection, including Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1883). It was played at community dances for over two centuries in the same communities, making it a living thread connecting the colonial era to the present. The straightforward D major reel structure — clear 8-bar strains, symmetrical phrasing — is ideal for contradancing with large numbers of couples.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by John Baltzell, digitized by the Internet Archive.
notes: D major with a formal, stately quality that reflects its Scottish courtly origins. Play it with precision and flow: clean string crossings, even 8th notes, no rushing. New England style calls for less ornament than Irish style but more drive than the parlor version. This tune has been played continuously for over 200 years in New England — treat it with appropriate respect. Good for contra dance callers because the phrases are mathematically even and the melody is memorable after one hearing.
audio_source: John Baltzell & John F. Burckhardt via Internet Archive

title: Glise a Sherbrooke
description:
Sherbrooke is a city in the Eastern Townships of Quebec, a region settled by both French Canadians and English-speaking Loyalists after the American Revolution. The French-Canadian fiddle tradition — driven by Catholic social culture, parish dances, and a rich repertoire of reels, jigs, and hornpipes — is one of the oldest continuous fiddle traditions in North America. Quebec fiddlers like Joseph Allard and Jean Carignan developed a highly ornamented, technically demanding style that influenced players throughout the Northeast.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by Ralph Page's New Hampshire Orchestra, digitized by the Internet Archive.
notes: A French-Canadian reel with a distinctive gliding character — 'glise' means 'glide' or 'slide' in French. The bowing should emphasize smooth connections between notes, with strategic slurs that give it a flowing quality. This is a tune where the phrasing matters as much as the notes. Quebec fiddlers play it with a characteristic lilt that Old-Time players often approximate.
audio_source: Ralph Page's New Hampshire Orchestra via Internet Archive

title: Lady of the Lake
description: Inspired by Sir Walter Scott's enormously popular 1810 epic poem 'The Lady of the Lake,' set in the Scottish Highlands, this waltz rode the wave of Romantic-era Scottish cultural enthusiasm that swept both Britain and America in the early 19th century. Scott's poem was so influential that it sparked a tourism boom in the Scottish Highlands and influenced countless folk tunes, songs, and dances named for its characters. The tune circulated in parlor music collections throughout the 19th century.
notes: A graceful, aristocratic waltz — the bow should float, never dig. The 3/4 rhythm should feel like breathing, not counting. Let the phrases arc up and back down. This tune rewards a slow tempo and a long, smooth bow. It's a formal dance piece from the parlor tradition; bring some courtliness to it.

title: Fisher's Hornpipe
description:
Composed by Johann Fischer (c.1733–1800), a German-born musician who settled in London, 'Fisher's Hornpipe' was published around 1780. It crossed the Atlantic and was embraced in New England contradance and Southern fiddle traditions alike. The hornpipe style — originally a sailor's dance — features characteristic dotted rhythms that distinguish it from reels. Thompson's 'Compleat Collection of 200 Favourite Country Dances' preserves early versions.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by WM. B. Houchens, digitized by the Internet Archive.
tags: hornpipe, dotted rhythm, english origin, widespread
notes: The defining feature of hornpipe style is the dotted rhythm — long-short, long-short. Don't rush the dots; hornpipes should feel stately, not scrambled. Fisher's has an elegance that rewards clean bow changes. The B part has a descending run that should flow smoothly. Many fiddlers add a slight pause at phrase endings in traditional style.
audio_source: Wm. B. Houchens via Internet Archive (1924)

title: Temperance Reel
description: The American temperance movement of the 19th century was one of the most powerful social reform campaigns in US history, culminating in Prohibition (1920–1933). Temperance groups often used popular fiddle tunes at their meetings to draw crowds, renaming them with morally improving titles. 'Temperance Reel' is one of several tunes that acquired teetotaling associations while remaining stubbornly associated with dancing and festivity.
notes: A tune whose name was borrowed by the temperance movement for anti-alcohol campaigns — play it with cheerful defiance. The reel is bright and quick, with a clear two-part structure. Keep the bow light and let the phrases bounce. Despite its abstemious name, this tune has always sounded better at a dance where someone has brought a jug.

title: New Five Cents
description: The 'new five cents' likely refers to the Buffalo nickel (Indian Head nickel), introduced in 1913, which replaced the Liberty Head design and became immediately popular for its artistic merit. The coin featured a Native American portrait on the obverse and an American buffalo (bison) on the reverse, designed by sculptor James Earle Fraser. In folk music, naming tunes for currency ('Two Bits,' 'Dollar Tune') was a common device suggesting either the tune's value or its association with pay-day celebrations.
tags: contra dance, new england, bright, clean
notes: A reel with the jaunty confidence of new money — the 1913 nickel (the Buffalo nickel) was a point of national pride. Keep the rhythm bright and forward-moving. The two-part structure is clear and well-defined; don't blur the seam between A and B. A good tune for building speed at jam sessions because the form is predictable.

title: Cotton-Eyed Joe
description: One of the most geographically widespread tunes in American folk music, 'Cotton-Eyed Joe' appears in both pre-Civil War minstrelsy and post-war Southern fiddle traditions. The lyrics reference an itinerant worker with eye disease. John A. Lomax collected it in Texas in the 1930s. The tune diverged into regional styles: a driving Appalachian version and a more elaborate Texas contest version.
notes: The Texas contest version is much faster and more ornamented than the Appalachian version — know which one your jam group plays. The A part uses a repetitive hook that makes it easy to learn but hard to play with real drive. Keep the drone strings ringing and accent the offbeats lightly. In Texas style, add quick slides into notes.

title: Mississippi Sawyer
description:
'Mississippi Sawyer' was first documented in print in the 1880s but is certainly older. The sawyer — a submerged log that bobs up and down in a river current — was one of the greatest hazards of 19th-century river navigation. Mark Twain described their dangers on the Mississippi. The tune's powerful, forward-driving character seems to capture the rhythm of a great river. It appears in multiple Southern fiddle collections.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by Don Richardson, digitized by the Internet Archive.

title: Bile Them Cabbage Down
alternative_titles: Boil Them Cabbage Down
description: 'Bile Them Cabbage Down' has been teaching new fiddlers to hold a bow for well over a century. The title refers to boiling (or 'biling' in Appalachian dialect) cabbage — a dietary staple of mountain households through autumn and winter. The tune appears in Southern collections from the 19th century and was played at community gatherings as both dance music and an informal teaching tool, since the two-part pentatonic structure in D major is almost entirely playable in first position with no complex string crossings. Its famous lyrics — 'Bile them cabbage down, boys / Bake them hoe-cakes brown / The only song that I can sing is bile them cabbage down' — exemplify the functional simplicity of mountain social song, where the text exists to give the room something to sing while the fiddler drives the dance.
notes: Start every new student on this tune. D major, first position, no fancy stuff. The bow should move evenly from frog to tip on the long notes; the short notes should be crisp. Singing the words while playing teaches phrasing more effectively than any metronome. For more advanced players, try adding open-string drones under the melody and see how many double-stops you can work in without losing the flow. This is also a perfect singing lesson tune.

The lowered 7th gives it a modal quality that distinguishes it from major-key reels. It appears in O'Neill's 'Music of Ireland' (1903) and has been collected across Appalachia under dozens of names.

The recording heard here is by Ian Jacks and Tom Joad, preserved by the Internet Archive.

audio_source: Ian Jacks and Tom Joad via Internet Archive (2000)

title: Sourwood Mountain
description: Named for the Sourwood tree (Oxydendrum arboreum), a native Appalachian tree prized for its honey and autumn color, 'Sourwood Mountain' is one of the most widely-collected Old-Time songs. Cecil Sharp documented it in his 'English Folk Songs from the Southern Appalachians' (1917), noting its popularity across western North Carolina and Virginia. The sourwood's late-summer blooming — when mountain bees produce distinctive sourwood honey — marked a seasonal moment in the Appalachian agricultural calendar.
notes: A song-tune with a strong, singable hook. 'Chickens a-crowing on Sourwood Mountain, hey-ho-dee-dee-dee.' Keep the rhythm lively and the melody bright — this is a courting song with a good-natured energy. The A major setting gives it warmth. Many players add open-string drones on the long notes. Great for contradances and social gatherings.

title: Cumberland Gap
description:
Cumberland Gap — the natural passage through the Cumberland Mountains at the convergence of Virginia, Kentucky, and Tennessee — was the gateway for hundreds of thousands of settlers pushing west through the Appalachians in the late 18th century. Daniel Boone blazed the Wilderness Road through it in 1775. The tune, named for this frontier passage, became a symbol of westward expansion and was collected widely across the South.

A field recording of this tune by Henry Reed was made for the Library of Congress in 1967 (American Folklife Center).
notes: A natural first tune for beginners — simple structure, open-string drones, and a memorable hook. Keep the bow arm relaxed and let the open strings ring between notes. The tune sounds great at moderate speed with hard downbows on beat one. Once comfortable, try adding a drone note below the melody on the repeat.

title: Hawk's Got a Chicken
description: Chicken hawks (red-tailed hawks, Cooper's hawks) were a genuine menace to Appalachian farmsteads, regularly taking chickens from the yard in the sudden, devastating strike that gave this tune its name. Farmers went to considerable lengths to protect their flocks. In the folk imagination, the hawk became a symbol of sudden loss and the unpredictability of rural life. Animal-hunt tunes — 'Fox Chase,' 'Hawk's Got a Chicken,' 'Cat's Got the Measles' — formed a whole genre of narrative fiddle music.
notes: A dramatic, predator-energy tune — the hawk's strike should be felt in the rhythm. Keep the bow arm sharp and decisive. The syncopated rhythm suggests the sudden, violent swoop of a hawk on unsuspecting poultry. This is a great uptempo showstopper. Don't smooth out the edges; the roughness is part of the character.

title: Cackling Hen
description:
An imitative tune that mimics the sounds of a cackling hen. A favorite for trick fiddlers and a demonstration of how Old-Time music imitates rural farm life.

The recording heard here is by Doc Watson, Clint Howard, and Fred Price, preserved by the Internet Archive.
tags: imitative, trick fiddling, farm life, humorous
notes: The staccato ornaments imitate clucking — play them bright and short.

title: Golden Slippers
alternative_titles: Oh Dem Golden Slippers
description: Written by James A. Bland (1854–1911), one of the most successful African American songwriters of the 19th century, 'Oh Dem Golden Slippers' (1879) sold over 100,000 sheet music copies within a year of publication. Bland wrote over 700 songs, including 'Carry Me Back to Old Virginny.' The fiddle tune version stripped the song to its essence and became a parade and dance hall standard across the American South.
notes: The minstrel origins of this tune don't change the fact that it swings beautifully. Play it with a light, buoyant bow — don't dig in. The verse and chorus have different feels; the chorus lifts. This tune adapted naturally into the fiddle tradition because the melody is so strong. Listen to early recordings to hear the swagger it carries.
audio_source: Vernon Dalhart & Carson Robison via Internet Archive (1927)

title: Ida Red
description: 'Ida Red' is one of the most historically consequential tunes in American music — Chuck Berry acknowledged it as a primary inspiration for 'Maybellene' (1955), his debut hit that effectively invented rock and roll's guitar vocabulary. The fiddle tune itself dates from at least the 1930s and was recorded by Bob Wills and His Texas Playboys among many others; Wills's versions helped establish the 'Ida Red' groove as a Western swing staple. Earlier still, the tune appears in the oral tradition as a Southern breakdown, with a repetitive, circular melody that creates a driving, hypnotic rhythm especially effective at the medium-fast tempos typical of dance music. That same quality — the relentless forward pull of a melody that never quite resolves — made it a perfect foundation for Chuck Berry to build rock and roll on.
notes: The groove is everything. Find a tempo that feels inevitable — not rushed, not dragged — and lock into it. The melody almost loops back on itself; that circularity is intentional and creates the hypnotic quality that made this tune a rock and roll blueprint. A major with open-string drones. Keep the bow pressure steady and resist the urge to add too much ornament; the power of this tune is in its relentlessness. Play it until the groove finds you.

title: Ragtime Annie
description:
A fiddle tune that absorbed the ragtime craze of the early 20th century, 'Ragtime Annie' blends the older Southern reel tradition with the syncopated rhythms of 1900s popular music. The tune represents the constant dialogue between folk fiddling and commercial music — a two-way street that shaped American music throughout the 20th century. It has been recorded by artists across Old-Time, bluegrass, and Western swing traditions.

The recording heard here is by Richie Hass, preserved by the Internet Archive.
notes: The ragtime influence is in the syncopation — feel the offbeat accents in the A part without forcing them. This should swing, not march. The B part is more straightforward, providing rhythmic contrast. Many players add a slight drag on the syncopated notes to emphasize the ragtime feel. Listen to early 1920s recordings to hear how fiddlers absorbed the era's popular music.

title: Georgia Railroad
description: The Western & Atlantic Railroad (the 'Georgia Railroad' line) was built between 1836 and 1851, connecting Atlanta to Chattanooga and opening up the interior South to commerce. The Great Locomotive Chase of 1862, in which Union spies stole a Confederate train on this line, became one of the Civil War's most dramatic episodes. The tune captures the rhythmic excitement of the railroad age — one of the defining technological experiences of 19th-century American life.
notes: A late 19th-century tune with a locomotive feel — keep the rhythm absolutely steady, like a train on rails. The A part has a call-and-response structure; the B part is more melodic. This works well at sessions when you want to establish a solid tempo reference for the group. Don't rush the tempo; a locomotive moves at a constant speed.

title: Tennessee Wagoner
alternative_titles: Johnny Wagoner, Johnny Walker, Reel Marie, Texas Wagoner
description:
'Tennessee Wagoner' first appeared in print in the late 19th century but is certainly older, referencing the wagoning trade — freight transport by horse-drawn wagon — that was central to Appalachian commerce before railroads. Wagoners were significant cultural figures: independent, hard-living, often musical. The tune's relentless forward drive captures the rhythm of a loaded wagon on a mountain road.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by Sleepy Marlin, digitized by the Internet Archive.

tags: driving, A major, bow technique, historical
notes: This tune has a confident, roadhouse swagger. The A part should feel inevitable — each phrase arrives like a wheel hitting a rut in the road. The B part offers rhythmic variation. Named for the wagoners who drove freight over Tennessee mountain passes, the tune's steady drive evokes long hauls and hard work. Keep the tempo rock-solid; this is not a tune for fluctuating tempos.

title: Billy in the Lowground
alternative_titles: Billy In The Low Ground
description: 'Billy in the Lowground' is among the most beloved C major tunes in the old-time tradition, with a name that places it in the landscape of the Southern lowlands — the 'lowground,' a low-lying field near a creek or river, often marshy, often the best agricultural land in a mountainous region. The tune is widely collected across the Appalachian mountains and has multiple variants across Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Kentucky. The name 'Billy' likely refers to a specific person known in the community where the tune was named — a common naming practice in the oral tradition — though no historical Billy has been definitively identified. The C major key is relatively rare in old-time fiddle music; most tunes favor G, D, or A, so 'Billy in the Lowground' stands out in any session for its distinctive harmonic color. The tune has been recorded by many artists including the New Lost City Ramblers.
