The two-part structure is symmetrical and the melody has a natural lilt that rewards a slight swing. Good for practicing intonation in a less familiar key. Don't rush the descending phrase at the end of the A part — that moment is the tune's emotional center.

title: Sitting on Top of the World
description:
First recorded by the Mississippi Sheiks (Walter Vinson and Lonnie Chatmon) in 1930 for Okeh Records, 'Sitting on Top of the World' became one of the most-covered songs in American music — recorded by Bob Wills, Doc Watson, Howlin Wolf, the Grateful Dead, Eric Clapton, and dozens of others. The Mississippi Sheiks were a Black string band from Jackson, Mississippi who moved fluidly between blues, Old-Time, and pop styles, reflecting the integrated musical world of the early recording era.

The recording heard here is by In House with Jeremy Petersen, preserved by the Internet Archive.
notes: A blues-influenced breakdown from the 1920s — the syncopation is essential. Don't play this straight; the rhythm needs to breathe and swing slightly. The lyrical version ('Was in the spring, one summer's day / When my good gal left me, she left me to stay') should be in your ear. A tune that lives at the crossroads of blues and country.
audio_source: In House with Jeremy Petersen via Internet Archive

title: Liza Jane
alternative_titles: Little Liza Jane
description:
One of the most widely-distributed African American song-and-dance tunes, 'Little Liza Jane' appears in print from the 1880s but is certainly older. Collected by John and Alan Lomax in multiple Southern states, the song was associated with ring plays, work songs, and dance music in Black communities. It crossed into the white fiddle tradition through the shared musical culture of the rural South and became a standard of both Old-Time and early bluegrass music.

A field recording of this tune by Henry Reed was made for the Library of Congress in 1967 (American Folklife Center).
notes: A classic song-tune — sing 'Little Liza Jane' in your head as you play. The melody has a natural lift and bounce that should carry through the bow. Keep the rhythm slightly syncopated in the A part for maximum groove. This is a tune that wants to be played loud and with confidence. Great opener for a jam — simple enough for beginners, satisfying for advanced players.

title: Old Sledge
description: Old Sledge (also called Seven Up, High-Low-Jack, or All Fours) was the dominant card game of colonial and early American society, played in taverns, on riverboats, and at social gatherings throughout the South and West. The game, brought from England in the 17th century, was widely played by all social classes. Games named for cards and gambling — 'Old Sledge,' 'Poker Night,' 'Faro' — reflect the central role of social gaming in pre-radio rural entertainment culture.
tags: card game, history, G major, driving
notes: A breakdown named for a card game — 'Seven Up' or 'Old Sledge' was the most popular American card game from the 1600s through the mid-19th century. Play with the quick, decisive energy of a card player laying down a winning hand. The rhythm should be sharp and articulate, not smooth. Good tune for demonstrating clean string crossings.

title: Whiskey in the Jar
alternative_titles: We'll Fight For Uncle Sam
description:
One of the oldest surviving Irish folk songs, 'Whiskey in the Jar' tells the story of an Irish highwayman betrayed by his lover. Versions appear in print from the early 18th century. It was carried to America by Irish immigrants and naturalized in the Southern mountain tradition. Metallica's 1998 cover introduced it to a new generation, but the tune's roots are firmly in 300 years of Irish oral tradition.

The recording heard here is by Celtic Influence, preserved by the Internet Archive.

The G major key and simple structure make this accessible for beginners, but the singing quality takes time to develop. Many fiddlers ornament the long notes with gentle vibrato or a bow accent.

title: Sweet Sunny South
description:
A song of post-Civil War Southern nostalgia, 'Sweet Sunny South' was written in the 1850s and achieved enormous popularity after the Civil War as a vehicle for Lost Cause sentiment. Henry Reed's LOC recording (afcreed000154) captures a Virginia fiddler's version that strips it to its essential melody. The 'Sunny South' was a complex cultural symbol — representing both genuine homesickness and the idealization of an antebellum past that obscured its brutalities.

A field recording of this tune by Henry Reed was made for the Library of Congress in 1966 (American Folklife Center).
tags: waltz, civil war, parlor, nostalgic, slow
notes: A Southern waltz with genuine tenderness — play it with a long, sustained bow and real feeling. The 'Sweet Sunny South' was a nostalgia trope in post-Civil War Southern culture: a longing for a pre-war life that was partly real, partly mythologized. Let that bittersweet quality come through. Three-quarter time should feel like breathing.

title: Aragon Mill
description: A haunting D minor tune about a textile mill closing in Aragon, Georgia. One of the great labor songs of the New Lost City Ramblers era.
tags: labor song, mill town, haunting, georgia, new lost city ramblers
notes: Play this with weight and sadness — it's a mourning song for a lost community.

title: Whoa Mule
description: Mule humor was a staple of Southern folk culture — the animal's stubbornness, strength, and occasional unpredictability made it a natural comic subject. 'Whoa Mule' joins 'Flop-Eared Mule,' 'Kicking Mule,' and 'Goodbye Old Paint' in the category of working-animal tunes that celebrated the central role of draft animals in pre-mechanized Southern agriculture. The mule (a hybrid of horse and donkey) was preferred over horses for farm work in the South because of its endurance and disease resistance.
notes: A comic, mule-themed breakdown with an insistent energy — the mule won't stop, and neither should the fiddler. Keep the tempo steady and the bow arm driving. The humor comes from the relentless forward motion that mirrors the tune's subject. A good session opener when you want to set a strong, clear tempo.

title: Blue Railroad Train
description: Railroad tunes were among the most popular genres in early commercial country music — the train was the defining technology of the era, connecting isolated communities to the wider world and carrying both hope and heartbreak. 'Blue Railroad Train' reflects the early 20th-century recording industry's fascination with train imagery, which appeared in hundreds of songs from the Carter Family, Jimmy Rodgers, and countless regional artists.
notes: A train tune — keep the rhythm as steady as a locomotive. The 'blue' in the title suggests a mournful quality beneath the driving rhythm. Don't rush; a train moves at a constant, powerful pace. The breakdown character suits both contest playing and informal session settings. Listen for the rhythmic 'chug' underneath the melody.

title: Kitchen Breakdown
description: A Southern kitchen dance tune — the melody has a cheerful, domestic quality suggesting informal dancing in front of a wood stove.

title: Big Sandy River
description: Named for the Big Sandy River that forms the border between Kentucky and West Virginia, this reel captures the rolling landscape of the region. The Big Sandy watershed was heavily settled by Scots-Irish families in the late 18th century who brought their fiddle traditions with them. The tune's smooth, rolling character evokes the river itself — wide, steady, and deep.
notes: A rolling, river-smooth reel — let the bow float through the phrases without digging in. The G major key with open strings available as drones gives it a full, resonant sound. Keep the tempo steady; this tune's character comes from evenness, not excitement. At Midwest fiddle contests it's often played with a slightly more swinging feel than Appalachian style.

title: Hog-Eyed Man
description:
A sailor's song of the mid-19th century that made its way from American seaports into the inland fiddle tradition, 'Hog-Eyed Man' (also 'Hog Eye') was sung on sailing ships and collected by folklorist Carl Sandburg in 'The American Songbag' (1927). The 'hog-eyed man' — a rough, working sailor — represents the world of maritime labor culture. The tune's migration from sea to mountain demonstrates how American folk music traveled along trade routes.

The recording heard here is by John Sizemore and J.F. Collett, preserved by the Internet Archive.
notes: A song-tune with a comic, earthy character. Let the words guide the phrasing: 'A hog-eyed man is the man for me, hog-eyed man of Tennessee.' The humor should come through in the rhythm. Keep the bow light and bouncy in the A part. This was a sailor's song originally — play it with a rollicking, shipboard swagger.
audio_source: Sizemore, John; Collett, J.F. (Farmer) via Internet Archive (1937)

title: Lost Indian
description: Recorded by Henry Reed of Glen Lyn, Virginia for the Library of Congress in 1966, 'Lost Indian' is a modal pentatonic tune with an ancient quality that suggests Native American or very early Scots-Irish influence. The name evokes the contact zone between European settlers and Native American peoples in the Appalachian frontier. Similar tunes appear in both Cherokee and Scots-Irish traditions, raising questions about cultural exchange that musicologists continue to investigate.
notes: One of the great modal tunes — the pentatonic scale and open, spacious phrases give it a genuinely ancient feeling. Play slowly at first to feel the modal quality; don't rush toward the tempo. This tune breathes differently from major-key reels. Henry Reed's LOC recording is essential listening. Let the open strings sustain freely — the droning quality IS the tune.

title: Katy Hill
description:
Associated with the Round Peak area of Surry County, North Carolina — one of the richest veins of Old-Time fiddle tradition in America — 'Katy Hill' was named for a hill near the community of Katy in the Blue Ridge foothills. The Round Peak tradition, centered on the fiddle-banjo duets of Tommy Jarrell and Fred Cockerham, is known for its powerful, heavily bowed style that became highly influential in the Old-Time revival of the 1970s.

The recording heard here is a 78rpm disc by Blue Ridge Mountain Boys, digitized by the Internet Archive.

notes: Named for a landmark near Galax, Virginia, 'Katy Hill' has the muscular, hard-driving character of the Round Peak tradition. The bow arm should feel strong and grounded. The A part has a satisfying repetition; the B part breaks free. Tommy Jarrell and Fred Cockerham played this one together. Let the open G string drone freely in the A part for a full, powerful sound.
audio_source: Blue Ridge Mountain Boys via Internet Archive

title: Forked Deer
description: Named for the Forked Deer River in western Tennessee, this reel was a staple of the Tennessee contest fiddle tradition. The Forked Deer River — named by early settlers for its Y-shaped bifurcation — runs through Gibson, Madison, and Dyer counties in west Tennessee. The tune appears in early 20th-century fiddle contest records and was widely played in the Mississippi Delta and surrounding areas.
notes: A powerful D major reel with a characteristic hook in the A part that listeners remember immediately. The 'fork' in the title is reflected in the tune's structure — phrases that split and rejoin. Keep the bow arm strong and steady; this is not a delicate tune. The B part rises and falls dramatically. At Tennessee contests this was a staple that fiddlers used to showcase their command of the bow.
audio_source: Taylor's Kentucky Boys via Internet Archive

title: Flop-Eared Mule
description:
A comic fiddle tune from the Southern tradition, 'Flop-Eared Mule' belongs to the category of animal-named tunes that were popular at 19th-century dances and social gatherings — 'Old Grey Mule,' 'Kickin' Mule,' 'Hell Among the Yearlings.' The mule was the workhorse of Southern agriculture, and its cantankerous personality made it a natural subject for folk humor. The tune's unpredictable rhythm reflects the animal's stubborn character.

The recording heard here is by Bev Baker and Norman Combs, preserved by the Internet Archive.
tags: humorous, G major, family music, dance
notes: A humorous tune named for a mule with drooping ears — play it with that same ornery, unpredictable energy. The rhythm has a slight hitch to it; don't smooth it out too much. Great for parties and dances where the audience wants something fun. The open-string drones give it a raw, outdoor quality. Many fiddlers add a 'mule bray' ornament somewhere in the B part.
audio_source: Baker, Bev; Combs, Norman via Internet Archive (1937)

title: Big Scioty
description:
Named for the Scioto River (pronounced 'sy-OH-tuh') in central Ohio, 'Big Scioty' is a tune from the Midwest fiddle tradition. The Scioto Valley was one of the first regions of Ohio settled by pioneers coming from Virginia and Kentucky in the early 1800s — they brought their Appalachian fiddle traditions with them, adapting them to Midwestern contest and dance hall settings. The tune appeared in early Ohio fiddle contest records.

The recording heard here is by Gerry Dempsey and Tom Joad, preserved by the Internet Archive.
tags: ohio, scioto river, rolling, G major
notes: An Ohio fiddle tune with a broad, rolling character — the 'big' in the name should be in the playing. The Scioto River Valley was the heart of Ohio's early settlement, and this tune has the confident stride of a prosperous agricultural community. Keep the tempo moderate and the bow arm relaxed but firm. Works beautifully in a bluegrass or Old-Time context.
audio_source: Gerry Dempsey and Tom Joad via Internet Archive (2004)

title: Whistle Daughter Whistle
description: A traditional song-and-dance tune of British origin that entered the American folk tradition through the 18th-century immigration period, 'Whistle Daughter Whistle' belongs to the comic song category where children and parents negotiate amusingly. The whistling tradition was an important musical skill in pre-instrument rural communities — field hollers, work signals, and entertainment all relied on the whistled voice. The tune was collected in multiple American versions by Cecil Sharp and later by Alan Lomax.
notes: A song-tune with a comic premise — a daughter who won't whistle until she gets something in return. The playful, negotiating energy should come through in the rhythm. Keep it light and bouncy. The simple pentatonic melody makes it accessible for beginners while the song character gives experienced players room for storytelling.

title: Mississippi Moon
description: The Mississippi River — 2,340 miles from Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico — is the great artery of American geography and imagination. Its moonlit surface appears in countless American songs, from Stephen Foster ('Beautiful Dreamer') to Mark Twain's descriptions in 'Life on the Mississippi' (1883) to Delta blues recordings. The waltz form — slower, more romantic than a reel — perfectly suits the languid, vast quality of the great river at night.
notes: A waltz with the wide, slow sweep of a Southern river under a full moon — let the bow float with maximum length and minimal pressure. The 3/4 time should feel absolutely natural and expansive. Don't rush; the Mississippi moves slowly. This is a tune where tone quality is everything — a singing, sustained sound in the upper register.

title: Colored Aristocracy
description: A Missouri breakdown from the post-Civil War era. The bright D major melody contrasts with the fraught history of its title.
tags: missouri, civil war era, D major, historical

title: John Henry Blues
description: John Henry is the great American labor hero — a Black railroad worker who is said to have driven steel faster than a steam hammer at the Big Bend Tunnel on the Chesapeake & Ohio Railway in West Virginia around 1870, then died of exhaustion. The story, whether historical or mythological, became one of the most widely recorded songs in American music. John Henry represented Black workers' dignity, strength, and resistance to industrial dehumanization. Guy Johnson's 1929 study 'John Henry: Tracking Down a Negro Legend' began the scholarly inquiry that continues today.
tags: john henry, blues, folk hero, G major
notes: One of America's great folk heroes — play this with the weight and resolve of a steel-driver. The blues quality should come through in the slightly bent notes and the heavy rhythmic pulse. Don't play this light; John Henry died swinging a hammer, and the music should carry that gravity. A slow-to-medium tempo reveals the character.

title: If I Hadn't Been A Fool
description:
The most documented recording of this tune comes from Vee V. Latty, a Missouri old-time fiddler. Vee V. Latty was born near Fulton, Callaway County, Missouri, in 1910 and began playing fiddle at the age of ten. "If I Hadn't Been a Fool, I Might Have Been a Lady" appears on his recorded repertoire, suggesting it was part of the Missouri old-time fiddle tradition in the early-to-mid 20th century.

He won the 1927/28 Missouri state fiddling championship, broadcast on WOS radio station out of Jefferson City, competing first on October 28, 1927, against 52 fiddlers from north of the Missouri River. Another 53 fiddlers from south of the river competed on November 25th, with the contest culminating in a championship on December 30 that pitted five winners from each side of the river against each other.

Latty was invariably accompanied by his wife Marie, playing an electric Hawaiian guitar, and they were sometimes joined by their son Wayne on guitar. He openly acknowledged his wife's contribution, stating after winning the 1927 championship: "I want to give my wife a great deal of credit for my success." Vee Latty died in 1956.

title: Hop Scotch Polka
description:
The foundation of "Hop-Scotch Polka" is a piece called "Scotch Hot," composed by an eccentric British performer named Billy Whitlock early in the 20th century. The song was originally recorded on a cylinder by the Edison Bell Gramophone Company with a special set of glockenspiel-like musical bells. Whitlock made an acetate recording in 1924, and it went virtually unnoticed for decades.

The story of how "Scotch Hot" became "Hop-Scotch Polka" is a classic tale of musical resurrection:
Two DJs played the song over and over and became obsessed with finding Whitlock and updating the number. After searching far and wide, they found the former entertainer in a lonely boarding house in Brixton, England, where he was working as a night watchman.
He was ecstatic to have his song revived. Gene Rayburn convinced Carl Sigman to write lyrics, and the result became known as "Hop-Scotch Polka (Scotch-Hot)."

"Hop-Scotch Polka (Scotch Hot)" is a popular song based on the Billy Whitlock composition "Scotch Hot," with new lyrics added by Gene Rayburn and Carl Sigman. The song was published on July 6, 1949, by Cromwell Music, Inc., and was soon recorded by several artists, including Art Mooney.

title: Uncle Dink
description:
"Uncle Dink" comes from the playing of fiddler Gene Goforth (1921–2002), of Eminence, Missouri, documented from a recording made by Mark Wilson in 1997.

The tune is named for Gene's father, Richard "Dink" Goforth, himself a fiddler.

The Goforths represent a deep, multigenerational fiddling tradition rooted in the Missouri Ozarks:
Dink left home when he was 15 years old and "did a little hoboing," but returned to Shannon County.
Dink's father, Josh Goforth, was also a fiddler — making this at least a three-generation fiddling lineage: Josh → Dink (Richard) → Gene.

title: Hold Old Bald While I Dance With Josie
description:
The tune is sourced from Jim Herd (1919–2002), originally from Missouri. It was recorded on Rounder 0437, the album Jim Herd – Traditional Fiddle Music of the Ozarks, Vol. 3 (released 2000), and has been transcribed and notated in the Traditional Tune Archive by Andrew Kuntz.
The tune is in the key of C major, a cut-time reel, and is firmly rooted in the Ozarks fiddle tradition.
It is listed on [Slippery Hill](https://www.slippery-hill.com/recording/hold-old-bald-while-i-dance-josie), the premier old-time recording database.

The title contains two puzzles: "Bald" and "Josie." The word josie appears across several related old-time tunes (like "Josie Girl" / "Josie-O") and has multiple folk-etymology threads:

A josie has multiple meanings: a girl's or boy's nickname (as in the tune "Jim-Along Josie"), an overcoat originally called a joseph worn by a lady in the 1800s, a term for underclothes worn by enslaved people, and also a dance.

title: Pat The Budgie
description:
"Pat the Budgie" was composed by Graham Townsend (1942–1998), a fiddler from Barrie, Ontario, around 1960–1961.

The tune was named for a real budgie — a Budgerigar, a small parrot native to Australia — who used to perch on Graham Townsend's fiddle bow while he played. The bird's name was Pat, and Pat would literally sit on Graham's bow as he fiddled.

It is a reel in common (cut) time, set in the key of C major, with lots of stepwise melodic movement. The tune typically follows an AABBCC or AA'BB'CC' form.

title: Moccasin Reel
description:
"Moccasin Reel" was composed by Andy DeJarlis, born in Woodridge, Manitoba in 1916, who came from a long line of fiddlers on both sides of his family.

His great-grandfather was an early settler in the Red River Valley, where settlers acquired their fiddles by trading pelts with fur traders, many of whom came from Scotland — and thus was born the Red River Jig and the distinctive Red River Style of fiddling.

Steeped in this tradition, it is only natural that Andy's "Caribou Reel," "Moccasin Reel," "Whiskey Before Breakfast," "Woodridge Breakdown", and many other tunes would bear the stamp of his forefathers.

title: Mississippi Snag
description:
"Mississippi Snag Boat" is attributed to Bert Payne, a Kansas fiddler. It has been passed along in the old-time community through fiddlers like Spencer and Rains. The shorter title "Mississippi Snag" appears to be a variant name for the same tune or a closely related piece, and is associated with the Missouri old-time fiddling tradition — appearing on the album "Nile Wilson – Tiehacker Hoe-Down" (MSOTFA 202D), recorded by the Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers Association, which works to promote and preserve the traditional fiddle music of Missouri and the surrounding region.

The tune title draws on vivid Mississippi River navigation vocabulary. A "Mississippi sawyer" was a river pilot's term for an uprooted tree in the water which sways back and forth with the current (like a sawing motion), with the tree breaking the surface suddenly in front of a boat. River pilots had names for different types of snags, including sawyers, preachers, and planters, depending on how they moved. A snag generically referred to any submerged obstruction — a serious hazard for 19th-century river traffic. On the Mississippi, the problem was of such proportions that special government "snag boats" patrolled the river to clear these dangers. This real-world river culture was a rich source of imagery for folk tune naming in the 19th century.

"Mississippi Snag" belongs to a broader cluster of old-time tunes named after Mississippi River life and lore.

title: Idlewood
description:
There are two competing attributions in the old-time community:

1. Lynn "Chirps" Smith — The tune is widely credited as a fiddle tune by Lynn "Chirps" Smith. It is described as a great tune composed by Chirps Smith, and he recorded it on his album "Down in Little Egypt." He also has a version recorded at a dance included in his "home recordings," and goes by the username MidwestFiddler on the Fiddle Hangout forum.

2. Ed Haley — According to the Fiddler's Companion, the tune comes from Ed Haley, the legendary blind Kentucky fiddler known for his vast repertoire of unusual and complex tunes.
At least one player's version is based on the one from Billy Mathews' collection of tunes.
On the Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle resource, "Idlewood" is listed and attributed to Chirps Smith, dated January 30, 2016.
Players in the community feel that "Idlewood" should become well known — it's considered "much fun to play."
Some players note that Chirps' recording reveals a nuanced B part that is easy to simplify, though simplified versions work fine in ensemble/dance settings.

title: Maple Sugar
description:
MAPLE SUGAR. Canadian (originally), American; Two-Step or Reel. Canada; Ontario, Maritimes. USA; northern New York, Pa., Missouri. A Major ('A' part) & E Major ('B' {or 'C'} part) {Bain, Beisswenger & McCann, Bohrer, Phillips, Silberberg}: G Major ('A' part) & D Major ('B' part) {Bayard}: D Major {Perlman}. Standard tuning. AA'B (Perlman): ABB' (Bayard): AA'BB' (Bain, Beisswenger & McCann): ABAC (Bohrer/Kibler): AA'BB'CC'BB' (Phillips): AA'BB'AA'CC' (Silberberg). Composed in 1956 by Ontario fiddler Ward Allen (1924-1965), a professional fiddler who won contest after contest in Canada the 1950's and had a successful career playing on the radio. Allen played with Montana Slim, Wilf Carter ("the father of Canadian country music"), appeared on the Grand Ole Opry, and had a radio show on Frank Ryan's station CFRA in Ottawa, Canada. "Maple Sugar" was released by Sparton Records in 1956 as the 'B' side to the Canadian "Back Up and Push (2)", which was expected to be the stronger tune. However, "Maple Sugar" was to become a hit in Canada, and received some airplay in the United States as well. 

It is also a tune which has varied considerably in the vicissitudes of the 'folk process' and has even acquired a set of words. In addition to being a staple of 'down east' Canadian fiddling, it has been popular in northern New York and northern New England; as Vic Kibler (Hamilton County, New York) said, "At every fiddle contest they all played it." It was in repertory of Buffalo Valley, Pa., region dance fiddler Harry Daddario. Shetland fiddler Aly Bain's version (which he calls "traditional Canadian") is much superior to that collected by Bayard (which is really one strain which is modulated to another key), who thought it a strain of a song air transformed into a dance tune.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Trip To Durrow
description:
"Trip to Durrow" has been attributed to Irish fiddler Dan Cleary (1918–2004), of Ballinamere, County Offaly. Cleary was a multi-instrumentalist who played the uilleann pipes, piano, and tin whistle, and was a member of a number of céili bands in the mid-20th century — notably the Ballinamere Céili Band, which won All-Ireland titles in the mid-1950s.

This reel is named for the Irish village of Durrow. The village of Durrow is in County Laois, in the southeast part of Ireland. One way to get to Durrow is to travel from the Celtic Sea, up the River Nore, and then to the River Erkina — Durrow is located close to the confluence of those two rivers.

The tune's name may stem from Cleary's days as a young man with the Colmcille Céili Band, of Durrow, Co. Offaly, who played regularly in the Forresters Hall in Tullamore. This connection — a young musician making regular trips to Durrow to play céilí dances — is likely what inspired the tune's title.

The tune was recorded by The Johnstons in 1969 — with Mick Moloney on banjo — making it the earliest known recording. Many in the Irish traditional scene first heard the tune played by Paddy Moloney on the first Drones and Chanters LP, released in the 1970s. The oldest documented source, considering both recordings and transcriptions, dates to 1960.

title: The Shaskeen Reel
description:
"The Shaskeen Reel" is one of the most celebrated pieces in the entire Irish traditional music canon — a tune with deep geographic roots, fascinating linguistic archaeology, a chain of legendary performers, and a name that has sparked debate for over a century.

The word shaskeen is derived from the Irish seisgeann, meaning either a marshy country or fen, a truss of corn, or gleaned land. The precise geographic source of the name is debated:
The title is also thought to have come from the name of a river in County Longford, a tributary of the Inny near Ballymahon.
To speculate on its earlier origin, there existed an old, now-deserted village of Seascainn, part of the larger townland of Gabhlán near Doocastle in East Mayo, where apparently Michael Coleman travelled to a spraoi at 'Scanlon's house.'
Séamus Ennis, with his characteristic wit, once offered a more colorful definition: Seamus Ennis once introduced the tune in the Tradition Club by saying the word meant 'a red piece of flannel that was tied to the tail of a cow that had mastitis', according to Finbar Doyle, who points out Seamus sometimes had a "delicate conjunction with veracity."

The tune is also known as "Ballinakill Shaskeen," "Butcher's Brussels Reel," "Hag Behind the Fire," "Miss S. Treby's Hornpipe," and "Shaskeen Clog," and is associated with south County Leitrim, Ireland.

Supposedly, the tune was played by a piper from the area, but instead of being named for the musician (as is often the case), the melody was called by the place the piper lived.

title: Snowbird In The Ashbank
description:
A "snowbird" is a nickname for the dark-eyed junco, a species of ground-feeding bird that can be seen hopping around during migration season. To cope with the cold of winter, juncos seasonally increase their insulating plumage to stay warm, leading to the association of the "plumper" bird with snow. An ashbank refers to a pile or mound of wood ash — a common feature of rural homesteads — which retains warmth long after a fire dies down. The image of the title is a junco scratching around in a warm ash pile, mistaking it (or not!) for snow.

One fiddler, Masters, noted that the bird was in the ash bank, not on it as the title usually goes — and the tune is considered imitative of the bird's hopping.

The title ("Snowbird" or "Snowbird on the Ashbank") must have been evocative, for it has been applied to several — often unrelated — tunes in the upland South, Piedmont, and Midwest.

The name appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountain fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954, and it was listed as one of the standard tunes in a square dance fiddler's repertoire by A.B. Moore in his History of Alabama (1934).

title: Down Home Waltz
description:
DOWN HOME WALTZ [1]. American, Waltz. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB'. Composed by Buck White. Drew Beisswenger (2008) finds a similar melody in Samuel Bayard's Dance to the Fiddle (1982), an untitled waltz (p. 567).

Source for notated version: - Art Galbraith (1909-1993, near Springfield, Mo.), learned in the 1960's from the playing of local fiddler Warren Dykes and from a Canadian version [Beisswenger & McCann, Phillips].

Printed sources: -  Beisswenger & McCann (Ozarks Fiddle Music), 2008; p. 38. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 253.

Recorded sources: - Ridge Runner RRR - 0006, Buck White - "That Down Home Feeling" (1977). Rounder Records 0133, Art Galbraith - "Dixie Blossoms" (1981).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: My Cape Breton Home
description:
"My Cape Breton Home" was composed by Jerry Holland (February 23, 1955 – July 16, 2009), a fiddler who lived on Cape Breton Island in Nova Scotia, Canada. He was born in Brockton, Massachusetts, to Canadian parents — his father was from New Brunswick and his mother was from Quebec.

During his childhood, Holland was exposed to the music of the large Cape Breton expatriate community in Boston. He began to play the fiddle and step-dance at the age of five, and played at his first square dance at the age of six. He made his television debut in 1962 on the Canadian program Don Messer's Jubilee, and by the time he was ten years old, he was playing regularly at dances in the Boston area.

Holland's family made annual summer trips to Cape Breton, and he moved there permanently in 1975.

The tune was composed in 1988 by Jerry Holland, based in Inverness, Cape Breton, Nova Scotia — written for his father, to commemorate their mutual love for Cape Breton.

title: Abe's Retreat
description: Political commentary through fiddle tune titles was a long tradition in American folk music. 'Abe's Retreat' — naming a tune for Abraham Lincoln's supposed retreat from something — suggests Southern or anti-Lincoln origin in the Civil War era. Whether sincere political commentary or ironic nickname, the title places the tune in the contentious political culture of mid-19th century America. Many Civil War-era tunes used political figures' names as coded commentary on events of the day.
notes: A tongue-in-cheek political tune — 'Abe' is presumably Lincoln, and 'retreat' was the last thing Lincoln did. Play it with some irony and forward momentum. The breakdown character suits a moderate-to-fast tempo. A historically interesting tune whose title suggests it may have originated in Confederate-sympathizing communities.

title: Addie On The Sandbar
description:
Unfortunately, my searches did not return any specific results about the old-time fiddle tune "Addie On The Sandbar" — its origin story, history, or the fiddler(s) associated with it. This is not entirely surprising, given the nature of the old-time fiddle tradition itself:

"Addie On The Sandbar," like most old-time fiddle tunes, exists within an oral/aural tradition where lots of variations exist and nobody knows exactly where individual tunes came from.

In the old-time world, when people say a tune is "from" a particular fiddler, it typically means that person was the earliest known source, not necessarily the original composer.

These tunes were not quite written the way we think of composers writing — they were more communal compositions, shaped and adapted by many players along the way, sometimes borrowing phrases from other tunes, until they became almost unrecognizable from any original source. Players simply molded tunes they heard to their own liking.

title: Adrian's Hornpipe
description:
Bob Walters ADRIAN'S HORNPIPE.  AKA - "Adreon's Hornpipe." American, Hornpipe or Reel (cut or 2/4 time). USA; Missouri, Nebraska. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. The original name having been forgotten, the melody was called by Nebraska fiddler Uncle Bob Walters for his source for it, Boone, Iowa fiddler Fred Adreon1 (1871-1949) or Adrian (not ‘Adrian’, as is sometimes miss-heard). It was popularized through the playing of Walters and Missouri fiddler Cyril Stinnett. R.P. Christeson noted it from the playing of the former in November, 1949, and did not hear it again until 1968, when he heard a fiddler on a live TV program in Missouri play it.

Source for notated version: - biography:Bob Walters (1889-1960, Burt County, Nebraska) Christeson, Milliner & Koken, Phillips.

Printed sources: -  Christeson (Old Time Fiddler’s Repertory, vol. 1), 1973; No. 121, p. 87. Clare Milliner & Walt Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 4. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 178.

Recorded sources: - Marimac 9017, Vesta Johnson (Mo.) ‑ "Down Home Rag." Rounder 0529, Dwight Lamb – “Hell Agin the Barn Door” (2005).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: All Young
description:
ALL YOUNG. American, Reel (cut time). A Mixolydian. Standard tuning (fiddle).

Source for notated version: - Melvin Wine Milliner & Koken, Phillips. The tune was played by Melvin's great-grandfather, David S. "Smithy" Wine (1829-1909), and was passed down to his son John Nelson "Nels" Wine (who, while not a fiddler, whistled, hummed, and sang his father's tunes), to his son Bill Wine, Melvin's father. Family lore has it that "All Young" and "Rainy Day (2) (The)" were favorite tunes of Smithy's Drew Beisswenger, Fiddling Way Out Yonder, 2008).

Printed sources: -  Clare Milliner & Walt Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 7.  Stacy Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 14.

Recorded sources: - Marimac Recordings AHS #2 (cass.), Melvin Wine - "Hannah at the Springhouse" (1989).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Altamont
description: Altamont is a common Appalachian place name — meaning 'high mountain' — appearing in multiple Southern states. The tune is associated with the Galax, Virginia fiddle tradition and has circulated in Old-Time and bluegrass contests since at least the mid-20th century. North Carolina and Virginia fiddlers associated with the Galax region developed a clean, driving contest style that this tune exemplifies.
notes: A fast, bright reel from the Southern contest tradition — 'Altamont' suggests elevation and clear mountain air. Keep the bow arm confident and the tempo driving. This tune rewards careful attention to bow distribution across the phrase. Good for demonstrating clean string crossings at speed. At North Carolina contests it's often played at a blinding tempo.

title: (And) The Cat Came Back
description: Written in 1893 by Tin Pan Alley composer Harry S. Miller and published in Chicago by Will Rossiter, 'The Cat Came Back' began as a darkly comic novelty song with minstrel staging and problematic racial dialect. Its core premise — 'Old Mister Johnson' tries every increasingly absurd method to rid himself of a persistent yellow cat, and the cat returns each time — proved irresistibly funny and the song's structure, with its relentless chorus, gave it enormous staying power. The tune migrated into children's music, folk revival repertoires, and eventually old-time fiddle sessions, losing its minstrel origins along the way and becoming simply one of the great comic songs of American tradition. Fred Penner's 1979 children's recording introduced it to multiple new generations. The fiddle tune derived from the song retains the rhythmic bounce and inevitable return of the melody — the musical equivalent of the cat's refusal to stay gone.
notes: The melody's built-in humor is the whole point. The 'return' figure — when the melody circles back to the main theme — should feel inevitable and funny every time. D major, bright and bouncy. Great for singalongs: 'But the cat came back, the very next day / Thought it was a goner but the cat came back.' Don't overthink it. This is joy music.

title: Antelope Gap
description: Preserved through the playing of Texas fiddlers Howard Rains and Trish Spencer, who documented it on their recording 'Old Texas Fiddle,' 'Antelope Gap' is attributed to Texas fiddler J.W. Whatley. The tune found an unlikely second home in the Tucson, Arizona old-time jam scene, where it became a local favorite without spreading widely elsewhere — a reminder that regional tune ecosystems develop their own peculiar repertoires. Antelope Gap is a real geographic feature: a pass through ridgelines common in the American West, usually named for the pronghorn antelope that would funnel through such natural channels. Texas fiddle tradition draws from Appalachian, Cajun, and western swing influences, and tunes like 'Antelope Gap' sit in the overlap — rhythmically driving without the modal darkness of the deepest Appalachian repertoire.
notes: A major with a Texas-style drive — keep the bow moving and don't let it breathe too much. The tune has a straightforward AABB structure without the modal ambiguity of Kentucky or Virginia styles. Howard Rains and Trish Spencer's recording on 'Old Texas Fiddle' is the primary reference. Good for sessions that want Texas flavor between Appalachian sets.

title: Apple Blossom
description: Apple orchards were a cornerstone of Appalachian farm economies — apple butter, cider, dried apples, and apple brandy ('apple jack') were essential preserved foods and trade goods. The brief apple blossom period in late spring, when hillside orchards turned white and pink, was one of the most celebrated moments of the Appalachian seasonal calendar. Old-Time waltzes often carry the names of natural phenomena that marked the agricultural year.
notes: A waltz with the delicate, brief beauty of apple blossoms — play it lightly and without pressing the bow. The 3/4 time should float. Apple orchards were central to Appalachian farm life, and their brief spring bloom was a celebrated seasonal event. Keep the tempo unhurried and the tone as sweet as possible.

title: Apple Jack
description: 'Apple Jack' belongs to the large family of Appalachian breakdown tunes named for foods, drinks, and rural materials — a tradition that includes 'Cornbread and Buttermilk,' 'Sugar in the Gourd,' and dozens of others. Applejack — a fermented and distilled apple beverage that was the primary liquor of many mountain communities before commercial whiskey became widely available — was produced across the Appalachian region from the 17th century onward, especially in Virginia, New Jersey, and the Carolinas. The drink appears in numerous folk songs and references as a symbol of frontier self-sufficiency and social gathering. The tune itself is a rhythmic breakdown in the standard old-time AABB form, passed down through the oral tradition of Appalachian musicians whose names and specific origins are no longer traceable.
notes: C major breakdown with the driving quality that characterized Appalachian dance music. The two-part AABB structure is clear and symmetrical, making it easy to jam with first-time partners who can learn the form quickly. The name suggests something strong and slightly rough around the edges, which should inform your bow arm: pressure and confidence rather than delicacy.

title: Arrington's Breakdown
description: Named for Charlie Arrington, an in-demand studio and dance musician of the 1920s–30s who recorded prolifically during the first golden era of old-time recording. Arrington was a working fiddler in the Southern professional music world — playing dances, recording sessions, and bandstands — and his breakdown reflects the polished, driving style of musicians who needed to hold a crowd and a dance floor night after night. The tune was preserved in the oral tradition and documented by modern fiddlers including Chirps Smith (who learned it from Paul Tyler) and the Volo Bogtrotters. Like many named breakdowns, it represents the practice of naming tunes for the fiddler who popularized them rather than necessarily who composed them — attribution in the oral tradition was often about the best-known carrier rather than the original inventor.
notes: G major breakdown with a driving, danceable rhythm. Play it with confidence and a hard bow — this is professional dance music, not a contemplative piece. The structure is clear AABB. A good tune for building bow arm endurance because the rhythmic demands are constant. Learn the version from Chirps Smith's recordings if you can find them.

title: Art Wooten's Hornpipe
description:
ART WOOTEN'S HORNPIPE.  American, Reel. USA, Nebraska. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BBCCDD (Phillips): AABBCCDD (Christeson). See note for "annotation:Art Wooten's Quadrille" for more.

Source for notated version: - Bob Walters (1889-1960, Burt County, Nebraska) Christeson, Phillips.

Printed sources: -  R.P. Christeson (Old Time Fiddler’s Repertory, vol. 1)), 1973; p. 96. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 181.

Recorded sources: - Bee Balm 302, “The Corndrinkers.”

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Aunt Mary's Hornpipe
description:
AUNT MARY'S HORNPIPE.  Old-Time, Breakdown. USA, Missouri. D Major. Standard or ADae tunings (fiddle). AABB. "Aunt Mary's Hornpipe" is on Charlie Walden's list of '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes'. Christeson said he never heard the tune played outside of the Little Dixie area of Missouri.

Source for notated version: fiddler Vee Latty, (Little Dixie area, Missouri) Christeson.

Printed sources:  R.P. Christeson (Old Time Fiddlers Repertory, vol. 1), 1973; p. 60.

Hear Missouri fiddler John White (born 1936 in a farmhouse near Ethel in Macon County, Missouri) play  the tune at Voyager Records 1

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Baby Ben
description:
BABY BEN. American, Schottische. G Major. Standard tuning. AABB. From the repertoire of Alabama fiddler James Bryan.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Backstep Cindy
description: One of the most beloved tunes from the Round Peak tradition of Surry County, North Carolina, 'Backstep Cindy' is a three-part crooked tune played in high-bass tuning (ADAE — the G string raised a whole step to A). The Round Peak style, centered around the musical community of Tommy Jarrell, Fred Cockerham, and their neighbors, is characterized by heavy bow pressure, drone-string emphasis, and a rhythmic drive that prioritizes dancing over prettiness. 'Backstep Cindy' exemplifies these values: its irregular phrase lengths ('crooked phrasing') create a rhythmic surprise that experienced old-time dancers specifically enjoy, while the ADAE tuning opens up drone possibilities unavailable in standard tuning. The title's 'Cindy' connects it to the vast family of Appalachian dance songs featuring female names — Cindy, Sally, Nellie, Betsy — most of which circulated as both song and tune in overlapping communities. 'Get along home, Cindy Cindy / Get along home, I say' is the lyrical world the tune inhabits.
notes: Tune up before you start: ADAE puts the G string up a whole step, which gives you a ringing open A as the bass drone. The three parts (A, B, C) each have slightly different phrase lengths — don't try to regularize them. Let the crookedness happen. Play with the weight and bow pressure of Round Peak style: closer to the bridge, slower bow strokes than you think, more volume than you expect. A foundational tune for anyone learning the Round Peak tradition.

title: The Baltimore
description:
"The Baltimore" is a tune title that appears in several old-time and related folk traditions. Like many old-time fiddle tunes named after places, it likely took its name from Baltimore, Maryland — a major port city and, historically, a significant crossroads for American folk music traditions.

Baltimore has long been a hub for bluegrass and old-time music. As the coal industry declined in the mid-20th century, Southern migrants traveled the "Hillbilly Highway" north, bringing their string instruments to working-class neighborhoods in Baltimore. This migration embedded Appalachian fiddle traditions firmly into the city's culture.

Old-time music as a genre lays ancient African and Celtic folk narratives over different forms of the same four or five strings. Tunes named after cities — like "The Baltimore" — were a common naming convention, often honoring a place where a tune was popularized, first played at a dance, or composed by a local fiddler.

title: (On The) Banks Of The Ohio
description: One of the most recorded murder ballads in American folk music, 'Banks of the Ohio' tells the story of a young man who drowns a woman when she refuses to marry him. The earliest known recording was by Red Patterson's Piedmont Log Rollers in 1927; the ballad itself is anonymous and likely dates from the mid-to-late 19th century, circulating through oral tradition for decades before anyone pressed it to wax. Like many Appalachian murder ballads, it presents the killer's perspective without moral judgment, leaving the listener to supply the outrage. 'I asked my love to take a walk / to take a walk just a little walk / Down beside where the waters flow / Down by the banks of the Ohio' — the language is pastoral, almost tender, which makes the murder more disturbing. Bill Monroe, Olivia Newton-John, Emmylou Harris, Doc Watson, and dozens of others have recorded it. The Ohio River, which forms the boundary between Kentucky and Ohio, was a real and symbolically powerful geographic feature in the 19th-century American imagination — the line between slave and free states.
notes: A minor or D minor depending on the version, though many singers use C major for a brighter, more unsettling contrast with the dark text. The tune is a song-tune: let the melody breathe, follow the text rhythm, and don't rush the long notes. The fiddle version works well as an introductory solo before vocals, or as a slow dance tune. The simplicity of the melody is its strength — don't ornament it to death.

title: Banjo Tramp
description:
"Banjo Tramp" is an old-time breakdown in D Major, standard tuning, with an AA'BB' structure, associated with the Kentucky and West Virginia tradition.

The clearest documented line of transmission for "Banjo Tramp" runs through two legendary figures:

Ed Haley (the ultimate source):
The notated version traces back to Ohio fiddler Ward Jarvis, who learned the tune from the legendary blind fiddler Ed Haley of eastern Kentucky.

Ward Jarvis (the key carrier):
Jarvis was born in West Virginia in 1894 and was deeply influenced by Ed Haley. He later moved to Ohio for work in the 1940s, settling in Athens County.

title: Barndance Polka
description:
The tune "Barndance Polka" is attributed to Art Stamper, appearing in major old-time fiddle references including the Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes (compiled by John S. Lamancusa) and the Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle repertoire list.

Art Stamper (1926–2005) was a master traditional fiddler from Floyd County, Kentucky, rooted deeply in the eastern Kentucky old-time and country music tradition. He was closely associated with the musical heritage of the Appalachian region and was known for playing tunes with a distinctively rhythmic, dance-ready style — making him a natural source for a polka-inflected barndance piece. He recorded and performed with a number of traditional musicians throughout his career and is regarded as one of the key carriers of Kentucky mountain fiddle tradition.
Key: C major (as notated in the Gettysburg Collection)
Genre crossover: The title "Barndance Polka" signals a blend of the Anglo-American barndance tradition with the polka rhythm — a Central/Eastern European dance form that swept rural American communities in the 19th century, absorbed into old-time string band music.
Feel: Upbeat, 2/4 or cut-time pulse, ideal for square dancing or social dancing contexts.

The tune appears among 522 traditional old-time tunes transcribed from jams, source recordings, festivals (such as Clifftop and Rock Bridge), and workshops (Rocky Mountain Fiddle Camp, Swannanoa, Augusta, Fiddle Hell).

title: Battle of Cedar Creek
description: The Battle of Cedar Creek (October 19, 1864) was a major engagement in the Shenandoah Valley of Virginia, in which Union General Philip Sheridan rallied his army from near-defeat to a decisive victory over Confederate General Jubal Early. Sheridan's famous 'ride from Winchester' — twenty miles to reach his retreating troops — became an instant legend. Civil War battles in the Shenandoah Valley directly affected the fiddle communities of the region, and the war's memory permeated Old-Time music for generations.
notes: A march-like breakdown commemorating a Civil War battle — keep the rhythm military-steady and the tempo moderate. The A part has a marching quality; the B part adds some melodic relief. Don't rush; this is a commemoration, not a celebration. Let the weight of the history come through in the playing.

title: Bean Walker's Mile
description:
BEAN WALKER'S MILE. American, Reel or Polka. C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'AA'BB. Phillips notes the 'A' part is the same as "Dominion Reel."

Source for notated version: - Lynn 'Chirps' Smith Phillips.

Printed sources: -  Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 18.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Beaux Of Albany
description: 'Beaux of Albany' traces its roots to an 18th-century Scottish reel that made its way across the Atlantic and took root in the New England contra dance tradition before spreading south into the broader American fiddle repertoire. The Scottish original appeared under titles including 'The Braes of Auchtertyre' in collections from the 1740s onward. Its transformation into the American 'Beaux of Albany' — Albany being the capital of New York, a significant urban center in the early republic — likely occurred as the tune circulated through New England dance halls and meeting houses in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. The tune belongs to the 'reel' family that formed the backbone of New England contra dance music, characterized by clear 8-bar strains, symmetrical phrasing, and a drive suitable for long-formation dances with many couples. Its D-major setting gives it a bright, formal quality that suits its association with a city rather than a hollow or a creek.
notes: D major with the characteristic brightness and forward motion of a New England reel. The AABB structure is textbook — clear, predictable, and danceable. This is a good contra dance tune: the phrases are even enough for callers to work with and the energy sustains across many repetitions. If you're coming from an old-time or Appalachian background, the New England styling — slightly more 'civilized' than a mountain breakdown — asks for precise bow placement and clean string crossings.

title: Bell Cow
description:
The name comes directly from rural American livestock culture. The "bell cow" was the dominant cow of the herd, which was belled to keep track of distant ranging herds in the hills, since all other cattle would be grouped around the leader. Boys would be given the task of turning the cows out in the morning, then going out to listen for the sound of the cowbell in the afternoon to gather them home for the second milking of the day. Different sized bells (different timbres) would also help denote one's herd from a neighbor's.

One of the earliest American references to a bell cow comes from the diary of New Hampshire native Matthew Patten, who noted in his entry of May 3, 1767: "Our bell cow calved a bull calf."

"Old Bell Cow" is a song printed in Ethel Park Richardson's American Mountain Songs (1927). It was set in the key of G Major/Mixolydian in the Old-Time String Band Songbook (Oak Publications, 1964) by the New Lost City Ramblers (John Cohen, Mike Seegar, Tracy Schwartz, Tom Paley), who obtained their version from the 1928 recording by the Dixie Crackers. It was presented by the NLCR as a children's song, and has entered children's programming repertory on PBS.

title: Belle of Lexington
description: Despite its name suggesting Kentucky's horse-country capital, 'Belle of Lexington' is primarily associated with southwestern Virginia — specifically Grayson and Carroll Counties, the same densely musical region that produced Albert Hash, Thornton Spencer, and the broader Whitetop Mountain musical community. The definitive recording came from Emmett Lundy (1864–1953), the legendary Grayson County fiddler, who cut it as 'Belles of Lexington.' Lundy's archaic, powerful style preserved melodic and rhythmic elements that other fiddlers of the commercial era had smoothed away, making his recordings essential documents of pre-commercial Appalachian music. The tune belongs to the 'Smith's Reel' family and shares melodic material with the Irish hornpipe 'Kitty's Wedding' and the related titles 'Belle Election' and 'Hauling Home.' This Irish connection is typical of the Appalachian repertoire, where tunes crossed the Atlantic and then spent a century or more diverging from their source material.
notes: Emmett Lundy's recording is the primary reference and worth finding and studying. The tune has a formal elegance — a 'belle,' after all, suggests something refined — but Lundy played it with Appalachian grit that contradicts the prettiness of the title. F major with some chromatic inflections in certain versions. The B part has an Irish reel character that's fun to lean into. Let the bow arm drive.

title: Betty Baker
description:
BETTY BAKER 1. AKA and see "Indian Nation (4)." American, Reel (cut time). USA; eastern Kentucky, West Virginia. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB. Although the tune called "Betty Baker" is known as a "W.Va. standard," it was played (in more or less related versions) by a number of east Kentucky fiddlers, including Manon Campbell, Clyde Davenport, Ed Haley and Hiram Stamper (1893-1992), of Knott County.  The latter also played a tune he called "Indian Nation (4)" 1 that is a version of "Betty Baker (1)."  See West Virginia versions at "Betty Baker (3)." 

Source for notated version: -  Manon Campbell (Hallie, Letcher County, Kentucky, 1977) Titon. 

Printed sources: - Titon (Old Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes), 2001; No. 5, p. 36. 

Recorded sources:   -  Augusta Heritage Records 003, Ernie Carpenter - "Elk River Blues - Traditional Tunes From Braxton County, W.Va." Copper Creek CCCD-0196, Tom, Brad & Alice - "We'll Die in the Pig Pen Fighting."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Betty Baker (Over the Hill to Betty Baker)
description:
The tune gets its full title from an old folk verse attached to it. One version of the lyric reads: "I went down for to see Betty Baker, / She was asleep and the Devil couldn't wake her; / She wouldn't stir and her mother wouldn't shake her, / Long time ago." A shorter, more localized eastern Kentucky version was remembered by oral tradition: Grover Salyer recalled a verse: "Went over the hill to see Betty Baker, / She was asleep and I could not wake her." The "Betty Baker" of the title appears to be a stock folk character — a sleepy, unresponsive woman — rather than a documented historical person.

Although the tune called "Betty Baker" is known as a "W.Va. standard," it was played (in more or less related versions) by a number of east Kentucky fiddlers, including Manon Campbell, Clyde Davenport, Ed Haley, and Hiram Stamper (1893–1992), of Knott County.

The tune exists in at least two distinct versions documented in the Traditional Tune Archive:
Betty Baker [1] — An American reel in cut time, in D Major, from eastern Kentucky and West Virginia. Hiram Stamper also played a tune he called "Indian Nation" that is a version of "Betty Baker (1)."
Betty Baker [2] — An old-time air and breakdown in G Major, in standard fiddle tuning, with an AABB form. This version was printed in Ira Ford's Traditional Music in America (1940).

title: Bibb County Hoedown
description: Bibb County, Georgia was named for William Wyatt Bibb, Georgia's first governor (1817). Located in central Georgia with Macon as its county seat, Bibb County was part of the fertile Georgia piedmont that supported a prosperous agricultural economy. The 'hoedown' — originally a dance where participants stamped and clapped rhythmically — became a generic term for any vigorous country dance gathering. Georgia fiddle contest traditions were distinct from both Virginia and Texas styles.
notes: A Georgia breakdown with a strong, county-fair energy. Keep the bow arm driving and the rhythm absolutely steady. A hoedown was literally a dance at a farm gathering — communal, informal, and exuberant. This tune should feel like a crowd of people who've been working hard and are ready to dance hard too.

title: Big Eyed Rabbit
description: Animal-themed tunes were among the most popular in the Old-Time repertoire — 'Big Eyed Rabbit,' 'Rabbit in the Pea Patch,' 'Rabbit Where'd You Get Them Long Ears' — reflecting the rabbit's prominent place in both Appalachian hunting culture and African American trickster tales (Br'er Rabbit). The rabbit was a dietary staple and a figure of folk wisdom: always watchful, always ready to run, surviving through cleverness rather than strength.
notes: A comic, animal-themed breakdown with a loose, swinging quality. The rabbit's wide eyes suggest wariness and speed — keep the rhythm quick and light. Don't dig the bow in; let it bounce. This is one of those tunes that sounds better played with a little carelessness than with excessive precision. Great for large sessions.

title: Big John McNeil
description:
BIG JOHN McNEIL(L)/McNEAL. AKA and see "John McNeil's Reel." Canadian, American, Scottish; Reel. Canada, widely known. USA; New England, Missouri. A Major. Standard (or infrequently AEae) tuning (fiddle). AABB (Gibbons, Messer, Sweet): AABB' (Miller & Perron): AA'BB' (Bégin, Perlman, Phillips). Though now known as a Canadian standard it originally was a reel composed (as "John McNeil") by the brilliant Scottish fiddler Peter Milne (1824-1908), one of J. Scott Skinner's teachers and early playing partners, who earned his living playing in theaters until his opium addiction (he abused laudanum, originally prescribed for rheumatism) reduced him to busking on ferry-boats crossing the Firth of Forth. He died in unpleasant circumstances in a mental institution. John McNeil was a famous Highland dancer of the mid-to-later 19th century (see note for "John McNeil's Reel" for more). The melody was in the repertoire of Cyrill Stinnett, a fiddler who epitomised the 'North Missouri Hornpipe Style' of playing, who apparently learned it and other tunes from listening to Canadian fiddlers broadcasting on the radio from Canada. Indeed, an influential recording of the tune was made 'Down-East' Canadian fiddler Don Messer with his group the Islanders, early in the 1940's-among the first of the sides the group waxed. A very similar melody, or a version, is "Lord Ramsay's Reel." Perlman (1996) notes the tune is a popular tune on Prince Edward Island, and a favorite vehicle for stepdancing in Prince County, PEI, on the western part of the island. Irish fiddler Sean Maguire recorded the melody in the 1960's under the title "Betty's Fancy (2).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Big Sandy
description:
There are actually two distinct fiddle tunes commonly associated with the "Big Sandy" name in American traditional music. Here's a full breakdown:

"Big Sandy River" is credited to Kenny Baker and Bill Monroe, composed in 1963. It is primarily a bluegrass tune, written in the key of A.

Kenny Baker was Monroe's longtime fiddler with the Blue Grass Boys, and the tune reflects that virtuosic bluegrass fiddle style. It is considered an essential bluegrass fiddle piece, frequently appearing at jams alongside tunes like Lonesome Moonlight Waltz and Monroe's Hornpipe.

The tune takes its name from the Big Sandy River, which forms the border between eastern Kentucky and West Virginia — deep in the heart of Appalachian old-time and bluegrass country.

title: Bill Brown
description:
BILL BROWN. American, Reel (cut time). USA; Magoffin County, Ky. A Major. AEac# tuning (fiddle). AABB. An irregular tune (the 'A' part has eight repeated measures, the 'B' part four repeated measures) in repertoire of Kentucky fiddler biography:John Salyer (Salyersville, Magoffin County). It was named for the fiddler who played the tune. Jeff Titon (2001) suggests it might have been named after William H. "Bill" Brown, who was executed by hanging for the murder of Irish peddler Morris Hagerty in Morgan County, Ky., in 1855. Bruce Greene likened the tune to "Sugar in the Gourd," according to Bruce Molsky.  John Salyer

Source for notated version: - a home recording of John Salyer, 1941 or 1942, by his sons, Grover and Glen Titon. 

Printed sources: - Titon (Old-Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes), 2001; No. 8, p. 39. 

Recorded sources:   - Berea College Appalachian Center AC003, "John Salyer: Home Recordings 1941-1942" (1993). Rounder 0361, Bruce Molsky - "Lost Boy" (1996).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Bill Driver's Tune
description:
William "Bill" Driver was born in Eldridge, Laclede County, Missouri, and later relocated to Miller County, central Missouri, southwest of Iberia, where he spent most of his fiddling career.

His father, also named William Driver, was the son of a slave known only as Mandy Dixon or Dickson. William Driver Sr. was born in 1859 and adopted as a child by a family called Driver, the name he carried for the remainder of his life. When he died in 1934, Bill Sr.'s occupation was listed as Minister of the Gospel; he had been a Free Will Baptist preacher traveling the circuit.

Bill Driver is one of two African-American traditional fiddlers from the Central Missouri area who are still well-known.

A gifted musician, he had a keen ear, kept steady time, and played vigorously. His was described as "the best example of a strictly indigenous repertory" his collector knew of — whereas other Missouri fiddlers had their repertoires diluted with hornpipes, jigs, and reels from phonograph records or mail-order sheet music, Bill stuck with the music and style of his locale.

title: Billy in the Lowland
description:
"Billy in the Lowground" is one of the most enduring and widespread of American traditional dance tunes in the key of C, known throughout the South, Midwest, and West and even into the northern part of the United States. As with most such long-lived and widely disseminated reels, there is a tremendous variation of the core melody due to both regional style, musical style (e.g., bluegrass, western swing), and individual fiddlers' idiosyncratic renderings.

The American tune borrows motifs from British and Irish sources. Scholar Samuel Bayard traced its genealogy carefully. The tune originated in Britain as a slow 3/4 time song tune from c. 1710 or earlier, called "O Dear Mother (Minnie) What Shall I Do?" He sees the development of the tune as having then split into two branches, and during the 1740s a 6/8 "giga" or jig form was composed called variously "All the Blue Bonnets Are Over the Border." Later in the century the second branch was fashioned from the original 3/4 tune into a fast duple time (4/4) dancing air which went by several titles including "The Braes of Auchtertyre/Auchentyre," "Belles of Tipperary," and "Beaus of Albany." These latter tunes are the immediate ancestor of the "Billy in the Lowground" group of tunes in America.

The title's meaning is hotly debated. Several competing folk explanations circulate:
William of Orange: The tune is said to be Scottish in origin, and the title refers to William of Orange at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690, where a "deep swampy ravine" figured in the tactics of the battle.

title: Bitter Creek
description: Bitter Creek could refer to several geographic features in the American West and South — there are Bitter Creeks in Wyoming, West Virginia, and elsewhere — all named because their water was alkaline, sulfurous, or otherwise undrinkable. In Appalachian folklore, 'bitter' was used to describe situations or places that were genuinely difficult — bitter cold, bitter grief, bitter labor. Old-Time tunes with austere names often preserved an unflinching honesty about the hardships of rural life.
notes: A tune with an uncompromising name — 'bitter' in Appalachian parlance meant something difficult, hard, or genuinely unpleasant. Play it with some grit and don't try to sweeten it up. The modal quality enhances the sense of hardship. A tune that tells the truth about difficult experiences without melodrama.

title: Black-Eyed Susie
description: The black-eyed Susan (Rudbeckia hirta) is a wildflower native to eastern North America — its bright yellow petals and dark center made it one of the most recognizable flowers of the Appalachian meadow landscape. In Old-Time tradition, 'Black-Eyed Susie' refers to a young woman, likely dark-eyed and attractive. The tune appears in multiple collections from across the Appalachian region and has been recorded by dozens of artists from traditional fiddlers to modern string bands.
notes: A cheerful courting tune that's one of the most widely-played in the Old-Time tradition. Keep it bright and forward. The A part has an insistent, questioning quality; the B part answers with more confidence. This tune is great for beginners because the form is clear and forgiving, but it has enough character to reward advanced players who add ornamentation.

title: Black-Eyed Suzy-Anna
description:
The tune's lineage is remarkably deep. Musicologist Samuel Bayard traces the history of the tune back to the British Isles, beginning with a melody called "Rosasolis," set by Giles Farnaby (c. 1560–c. 1600), which appears in the Fitzwilliam Virginal Book.

Another version of the melody is called "Morris Off" and appears in Jehan Tabourot's Orchesographie (1588); it is still used for English morris dances and has been called the earliest recorded morris tune. Still another version appears as an old Welsh harp tune in Alawon Fy Ngwlad / Lays of My Land.

Later developments of the tune were popular in England and Scotland from the early 17th century through the 18th, under the title "Three Jolly Sheep Skins"; while in Ireland a variation became known as "Aillilliu mo Mhailin" (Alas my little bag) — a humorous lament for a stolen bag of sundries.

title: Black Jack Grove
description:
BLACK JACK GROVE 1. AKA - "Blackjack Grove." American, Reel. USA, Kentucky. A Mixolydian ('A' part) & A Dorian ('B' part) {Phillips, Titon}: A Mixolydian ('A' part) & A Major ('B' part) {Silberberg}.  Standard or AEae (McNew) tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberbert): AABB (Phillips, Titon). Phillips notes that his source, Walter McNew, tended to blur the 'C' notes in the 'B' part of his unaccompanied version, resulting in a tonality somewhere between minor and major. Jeff Titon (2001) finds the title in tune lists from Berea College in 1915 and in the 1919 Berea fiddle contest list. The title presumably takes its name from a locale with a  grove of blackjack oak trees.  

McNew learned "Black Jack Grove" from his father John McNew (b. 1888), a telegraph operator and depot agent for the L & N Railroad, who would play his fiddle between dispatches during the graveyard shift at his train depot. Walter learned the tune from his father, and thought that his father in turn had it from a man known to the family as 'Uncle' Garrett Bow, who used to visit with the elder McNew at the train depot where the two would swap tunes through the night 1 McNew was also highly influenced by neighboring Madison County, Ky., fiddler Doc Roberts, whom he knew and held in awe. 

See also "Blackjack", recorded in the field from the playing of Hobert Bowling by John Harrod and Mark Wilson (heard on Rounder 0544/Field Recorder Collective FRC731). For the musically unrelated Texas tune of the same name, see "Black Jack Grove (2)."

Source for notated version: - Walter McNew (1912-1998, Mt. Vernon, Rockcastle County, central Ky.) Milliner & Koken, Phillips, Titon

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Black Sally Goodin
description:
BLACK SALLY GOODIN. Old-Time, Breakdown (cut or 2/4 time). USA, Missouri. G Major (Christeson): D Major (Pete McMaham). Standard or GDad tuning (fiddle). ABC. "Black Sally Goodin'" is on Missouri fiddler and teacher Charlie Walden's list of '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes'. The title probably does not refer to an African-American female named Sally Goodin', but rather that the tune was played by Black fiddlers and absorbed into white fiddlers' repertoire. Describing it as 'Black Sally Goodin' differentiated the melody from other "Sally Goodin'" tunes and helped avoid confusion. 

Source for notated version: - African-American fiddler Bill Caton (or Katon) via his friend Vee Latty (Callaway County, north-central Missouri), who was recorded in the field in the 1950's Christeson. Bill Caton (or Katon) was an African-American fiddler who played regularly over WOS, accompanied on guitar by Ola Gaithright. Unfortunately no commercial or field recordings survive of Caton's playing.

Printed sources: - R.P. Christeson (Old Time Fiddlers Repertory, vol. 1), 1973; No. 134, p. 95. Bill Shull (Cross-Tuning Your Fiddle), 1994;

Recorded sources:   - Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers Association 001, Pete McMahan - "Ozark Mountain Waltz." JL 9601, Kim & Jim Lansford - "New Harmony".

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Black Satin
description: Satin — a smooth, glossy woven fabric with a silky texture — was a luxury textile associated with formal dress, ballrooms, and high-status social occasions in 19th-century American culture. 'Black Satin' as a tune name evokes the world of formal social dancing: polished floors, fine clothes, and carefully executed dance figures. The tune's smooth melodic character suits the material it's named for.
notes: A smooth, elegant tune that should sound like its name — silky and polished. Keep the bow arm relaxed and the tone round and warm. No roughness here. This is a tune for showing off clean intonation and smooth bow changes. Play it at a moderate tempo where the elegance can register.

title: Black Widow Romp
description:
The tune was written by Chris Romain (also sometimes spelled Romaine), from the DC area. He can often be found at Clifftop (the renowned Appalachian String Band Music Festival in West Virginia) with the other Roustabouts at the Elvis Shrine.

In Dan Levenson's "Buzzard Banjo" tab book, the tune is credited as being written by Chris Romaine. Some sources credit it to both Chris Romaine and Dan Levenson — a common occurrence in the old-time community where arrangers and compilers sometimes get co-credited alongside the original composer.

It appears to be a newly written tune, meaning it's a modern composition in the old-time style rather than a tune with deep historical roots stretching back generations. New fiddle tunes have always been written and are still being written today in the old-time tradition, so "Black Widow Romp" fits squarely in that living, evolving practice.

title: Blake's March
description:
"Blake's March" was written by Norman Blake. Norman L. Blake (born March 10, 1938) is a traditional American stringed instrument artist and songwriter, born in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and raised in Sulphur Springs, Alabama.

He grew up listening to old-time and country music on the radio — the Carter Family, the Skillet Lickers, Roy Acuff, and the Monroe Brothers — and learned guitar at age 11 or 12, then mandolin, dobro, and fiddle in his teens. When he was 16, he dropped out of school to play music professionally.

Though probably best known for his fluid renditions of classic fiddle tunes transcribed for guitar, Blake has also written songs that became bluegrass and folk standards, such as "Ginseng Sullivan," "Slow Train through Georgia," and "Church Street Blues."

Norman Blake's tune "Blake's March" was recorded on Original Underground Music from the Mysterious South (available on the compilation Natasha's Waltz) by the Rising Fawn String Ensemble: Norman Blake, Nancy Blake, Peter Ostroushko, Carl Jones, and Larry Sledge. It's a sprightly fiddle tune in the key of G.

title: Blue Eagle
description:
BLUE EAGLE. American, Reel (cut time). USA, Texas. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. A regional Texas tune not well known in other parts of the South. The tune has been attributed to fiddle player Orville Burns (b. 1921, Oklahoma, later moved to Texas), whose father suggested the name to him. The Blue Eagle was the depression-era symbol of a thunderbird, employed by companies to show compliance with the National Industrial Recovery Act.

Source for notated version: - Lewis Franklin (Texas) Devil's Box, Phillips; Gary Lee Moore (Seattle) Silberberg.

Printed sources: -  Stephen F. Davis (The Devil's Box), vol. 14, No. 3, Sept. 1980; p. 34. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 30. Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 13.

Recorded sources: - County 707, Lewis Franklin - "Texas Fiddle Favorites."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Blue Goose
description: The snow goose (Chen caerulescens) has a blue-gray 'blue morph' phase that gave it the folk name 'blue goose' in many parts of North America. Migratory waterfowl — geese, ducks, herons — were important food sources and harbingers of seasonal change in Appalachian culture. The Blue Goose was also a common name for country stores and roadhouses throughout the rural South, suggesting a warm, unpretentious gathering place.
notes: A tune with the unhurried, heavy quality of a goose in flight — keep the tempo moderate and the bow arm grounded. The Blue Goose was a real bird and a real brand, and the name suggests something solid and unpretentious. Don't rush this one. Let the open string drones carry.

title: Blue Mule
description:
BLUE MULE. AKA - "Old Blue Mule." AKA and see "Austin Breakdown." American, Reel (cut time). USA; Arkansas, Missouri. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): AA'BB'C (Beisswenger & McCann). "Blue Mule" was recorded for the Library of Congress by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph in the early 1940's from Ozarks Mountains fiddlers, where it is a regionally popular tune formerly seldom heard in other parts of the country. The tune may have had origins in a hornpipe and is structurally similar. Mark Wilson sees resemblance with the tunes "Nancy's Got a Pretty Dress On" and "Austin Breakdown," while Drew Beisswenger (2008) finds Absie Morrison's "Irish Washerwoman (2)" (a reel version) similar, particularly with the ending cadences. There is some speculation it may have derived from the play-party song "Skip to My Lou." "Blue Mule" is usually heard played in two strains. Source Glen Rickman (1901-1982) believed the tune to have been played during the Civil War, and identified his additional third part as the one a "Rebel" cousin had played Beisswenger & McCann. 

Guthrie Meade gives two early 78RPM recorded sources: Bob Miller's Hinky Dinkers (1930) and Jess Hillard & His West Virginia Hillbillies (1933). It was in the repertoire of Missouri fiddlers Art Galbraith (1909-1993, who said it was learned from older members of his family) and Bob Holt (1930-2004), and by Bill (Willie) Bilyeau for the Library of Congress.

Printed sources: -  Beisswenger & McCann (Ozarks Fiddle Music), 2008; p. 112. Silberberg (Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern), 2002; p. 13.

Recorded sources: - Rounder 133, Art Galbraith - "Dixie Blossoms" (1981). Rounder 0435, Bob Holt. Rounder 8041, Art Galbraith & Gordon McCann - "The Land of Yahoe."
