title: Fiddler's Reel
description:
FIDDLER'S REEL. Old-Time, Fiddle Tune. USA; North Carolina. D Major. Standard tuning. AA'BB'. Known as a Surry County, North Carolina, regional tune (it was in the repertoire of Benton Flippen [1] {1920-2011}, for example), the title also appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954. 

Source for notated version: Benton Flippen (Mt. Airy, North Carolina) [Milliner & Koken].

Printed sources: Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 195.

Alcazar Dance Series ALC 202, Sandy Bradley – "Potluck and Dance Tonite!" (1979).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Fireman's Dance Cotillion
description:
There are actually two separate tunes in the old-time canon that go by similar names, and they are worth distinguishing:

The Philadelphia Fireman's Cotillion is credited to Francis Johnson (1792–1844) and was composed in 1822. It is written in 2/4 time, in the key of C, and the notation source is the Fiddler's Companion.

Francis Johnson was a pioneering African-American composer, bandleader, and multi-instrumentalist based in Philadelphia. He was one of the most celebrated musicians in early 19th-century America and composed numerous cotillions, marches, and dance pieces for formal occasions — many of them with civic or topical titles, such as this one honoring the Philadelphia fire companies.

title: Five Miles To Town
description:
First, an important clarification: this tune is distinct from the Missouri "Five Miles Out of Town," Thede's "Five Miles from Town," and Clyde Davenport's "Five Miles from Town." Folklorist Jeff Titon (2001) worked to clear up "the dizzying confusion among the many similar 'Five Mile to/from/out of Town' titles." They are related in name but are different tunes with different lineages.

The tune most commonly called "Five Miles to Town" is sourced to John Sharp (1894–1964):
John Sharp was originally from Wayne County, Kentucky, where he was born in one of the oldest log structures in the region. He lived in Sharp Place, northeast of Jamestown, Tennessee, and was a logger and farmer who only lived out of the region once in his life, a short stay in Iowa.
Sharp and a neighbor, Virgil Anderson (a banjo player), formed a group called the Kentucky Wildcats and toured coal camps during the Depression, later settling into a routine of local gigs at dances, reunions, and rallies at Picket State Park.
He was recorded in the field on a home disc recorder in 1949 by his neighbor, World War I hero Sergeant Alvin York — who also recorded Sharp again in 1964, just before the fiddler died, on a tape recorder.
The tune was later printed in the Milliner & Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes (2011), p. 203.

title: Five Miles Out Of Town
description:
This title is a cluster of related but distinct tunes that have long confused collectors and players alike. Here's a breakdown of each variant, the key fiddlers, and what's known about origins.

There are actually several different tunes sharing similar names: the Missouri "Five Miles Out of Town," Thede's "Five Miles from Town," and Clyde Davenport's "Five Miles from Town" are all separate tunes. Jeff Titon (2001) directly addresses and clears up "the dizzying confusion among the many similar 'Five Miles to/from/out of Town' titles."

It is on Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden's list of "100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes" and has been recorded by such Missouri fiddlers as Cyril Stinnett and Dwight Lamb.
The notated version comes from the playing of Frame Davis (Des Moines, Iowa), recorded in 1950 by Bob Christeson. Davis was also a railroad engineer.
Another key source is Cyril Stinnett (1912–1986), a southpaw fiddler from Oregon, northwest Missouri. Stinnett was born near Savannah in northwest Missouri in 1912; his father was a farmer and a fiddler.

Minstrel Roots:
Hans Nathan (Dan Emmett and Negro Minstrelsy, Univ. of Oklahoma Press, 1962, p. 93) mentions that "Five Miles Out of Town" was the name of an old blackface minstrel dance or series of steps.

title: Flatfoot in the Ashes
description:
"Flatfoot in the Ashes" is grouped among West Virginia fiddle tunes that mirror favored traditional activities of rural Appalachian life — the title almost certainly evoking the old practice of flatfoot (buck) dancing near the hearth, with ashes on the floor used as a kind of dance surface or noise-maker under the feet.

The roots of West Virginia's old-time fiddle tunes lie in the Old World, with a heavy Celtic/Anglo connection among tune sources. African Americans also originated and/or influenced the blues, rags, and syncopated breakdowns that pervade old-time tune lists — influences that can be found in most American musical forms originating in the American South.

The tune is most closely associated with Harvey Sampson of West Virginia. It is played in A Modal with a cross-tuning of AEAE (the LP itself lists the tuning as GDGD). The canonical recording appears on the Augusta Heritage LP AHR 004 (1986), now out of print. Notes for the tune come from the collection of Gerry Milnes.

title: Ford's One Step
description:
The tune's name almost certainly pays homage to Henry Ford, whose enormous influence on the old-time fiddle tradition in the 1920s inspired a wave of tune-naming in his honor. Henry Ford loved music — especially the fiddle tunes he enjoyed at the country dances of his youth. As a young man, Ford bought an inexpensive fiddle and learned to play a bit. Though he was never able to play as well as he would have wished, his love of the fiddle and rural dance music remained with him throughout his life.

Ford needed a band to play at his "old-fashioned" dances, so he put together his "Old Time Orchestra" in 1924. In 1926, Henry Ford, who was greatly interested in old-time fiddling, held contests at his Ford dealership. He sponsored fiddle contests at dealerships in hundreds of communities across the country, and Ford's promotion of fiddling helped contribute to its growing popularity on the radio.

The tune's subtitle — "One Step" — refers to a popular early 20th-century dance form. Old-time fiddle tunes are derived from European folk dance tunes such as Jig, Reel, Breakdown, Schottische, Waltz, Two Step, and Polka. The One Step was a close cousin of the Two Step — a lively, syncopated social dance that surged in popularity during the ragtime era (roughly 1910s–1920s), making it perfectly suited to the fiddling revival Ford was championing.

title: Fork Horned Buck
description:
"Fork Horned Buck" is an old-time fiddle tune in the broader family of "Forked Deer"-related tunes — a cluster of American fiddle pieces sharing similar melodic DNA and titles rooted in frontier hunting culture. The name itself evokes the imagery of a two-pronged (forked) antler buck, which was considered a prize in the pioneer hunting world.

"Forked Deer" is a quintessential fiddle tune of the old frontier — old and widely distributed, yet it cannot be traced to the Old World or the northern United States.

Ira Ford's (1940) origin story traces the tune to the days of powder horns, bullet molds, and coonskin caps. It has been traced to the first settlers along the Big Sandy River, on the border of Virginia and Kentucky. In the family which preserved the tune, the story — handed down through several generations — credits authorship to a relative, a noted fiddler of pioneer days. This kinsman was also a famous hunter. There was a spirit of friendly rivalry in the hunt, and he had established a reputation as a champion deer hunter by always bringing in a forked deer. The forked deer, or two-point buck, was considered prime venison.

The tune is fiddled with a fluid bowing style using slurs to create complicated rhythmic patterns, in the manner of the old Upper South. Its title both evokes the forest and names a river in West Tennessee.

title: Fortune
description:
FORTUNE [1]. AKA- "Once I Had a Fortune." Old-Time, Song and Breakdown. USA, "most popular around Galax, Va." (Krassen, 1973). D Major. Standard or ADae tunings (fiddle). AB (Silberberg): AABB (Brody, Krassen, Kuntz, Phillips). Called a "Blue-Ridge Mountain standard," it is found in western North Carolina and southwest Virginia, but has become particularly identified with Galax/Hillsville, southwestern Virginia area, style bands. It was, for example, one of the few tunes recorded by legendary Galax, Va., fiddler Emmett Lundy, and Galax, Va., storekeeper, banjo and fiddle player John Rector was recorded playing "Fortune" in 1926 by collector John Lomax. Mt. Airy, North Carolina, fiddler Tommy Jarrell (1901-1986) said of the melody: "I can recollect hearing my daddy play it as far back as I can recollect. I don't know where that started from...it was more just an old, well, a flat foot dance tune I'd say." 

Once I had a fortune, I put it in my trunk,

I lost it all a-gambling one night when I was drunk.

Wish I had a pretty little hog/horse, corn to feed him on,

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Forty Drops
description:
FORTY DROPS [1]. Old-Time, Country Rag. F Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). ABAB' (Phillips): AABBAABC (Beisswenger & McCann). 

Sources for notated versions: - Jere Canote [Phillips]; Howe Teague (1913-2005, Dent County, Missouri) [Beisswenger & McCann].

Printed sources: - Beisswenger & McCann (Ozarks Fiddle Music), 2008; p. 148. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 52. 

Recorded sources:   -Gold Standard, Howe Teague - "Ozark Memories" (c. 1986).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Forty Miles From Georgetown Without Any Whiskey
description:
The tune is credited to Garry Harrison, as noted in the Traditional Tune Archive (TuneArch), where it is catalogued as a reel in the key of C, composed by Harrison.

Harrison is associated with the Indian Creek Delta Boys, and at least one fiddler reports having learned the tune directly from Garry Harrison at Fiddle Tunes in 1998.

The tune appears on a recording by the Indian Creek Delta Boys, documented in the collection Old Time Fiddling From The State Of Illinois. This firmly roots the tune in the downstate Illinois old-time tradition.

title: Frankie
description:
FRANKIE. Old-Time, Breakdown. USA, north-eastern Ky. A Major ('A' part) & D Major ('B' part). Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'B. The tune was in the repertoire of Buddy Thomas's grandfather, Jimmy Richmond, although Thomas learned it from the whistling of his mother. Mark Wilson (1976) notes that the tune is related to Pete Riley's tune "Rattlesnake" and to a tune called "Boatin' Up Sandy" played by a Portsmouth, Ohio, fiddler.  

Source for notated version: Buddy Thomas (1934-1974, Emmerson, Lewis County, Ky., 1973) [Milliner & Koken, Phillips, Titon]. 

Printed sources: Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 220. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 92. Titon (Old-Time Kentucky Fiddle Tunes), 2001; No. 46, p. 78. 

Recorded sources: Field Recorders Collective FRC 303, "Buddy Thomas: Recordings from the collection of Dave Spilkia & Ray Alden" (2015). Rounder 0032, Buddy Thomas (northeast Ky.) - "Kitty Puss: Old-Time Fiddle Music From Kentucky" (1976). Rounder SS-0145, Buddy Thomas (northeast Ky.) - "Traditional Music on Rounder: A Sampler" (1981. A different recording than on Rounder 0032).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Free State Hornpipe
description:
FREE STATE HORNPIPE. AKA - "Hornpipe in A," "Hilltop Hornpipe." Old-Time, Hornpipe. A Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. The hornpipe takes its name from a portion of Fauquir County, northern Virginia, that attempted to form a 'free state' to avoid paying taxes. 

Source for notated version: - Tommy Jackson and John Ashby [1] (1915-1979, Fauquier County, Virginia) [Phillips]. Ashby himself says the tune came from Winchester, Virginia, fiddler Ralph Lamp. 

Printed sources: -  Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 202 (appears as "Hornpipe in A"). 

Recorded sources:   -

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Full Moon Reel
description:
"Full Moon Reel" is credited to composer Mark Schatz, played by Ryck Kaiser, in the key of A, with AEAE cross-tuning. It appears in the Old Time Fiddle Tunes collection assembled by John Lamancusa, and is referenced in the Old Time Fiddling from the State of Pennsylvania / Gettysburg Collection under the category of Newly Written Fiddle Tunes.

This is a key detail: the tune is categorized as a newly written (i.e., composed) fiddle tune, not an ancient traditional melody passed down anonymously through generations.

Mark Schatz is a well-known bassist and old-time/bluegrass musician who has worked with Tony Rice, Nickel Creek, and many others. He is also an accomplished clogging dancer and tune composer. His background straddles the line between traditional old-time music and the contemporary folk/bluegrass revival world, which fits perfectly with writing new tunes in the old-time idiom.

title: Galleynipper
description:
GALLEYNIPPER. Old-Time. USA, Ky. A Major. Learned by northeast Ky. fiddler J.P. Fraley from his father. Guthrie Meade (1980) states this tune is associated with eastern Kentucky and West Virginia fiddlers. A galleynipper (or galley napper) is a crane fly, or, historically, a large mosquito.

Source for notated version: 

Recorded sources: June Appal JA 058C, J.P. & Annadeene Fraley - "Galleynipper" (1990). Rounder 0351, J.P. & Annadeene Fraley - "Maysville" (1995).

Back to Galleynipper

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Garfield's Blackberry Blossom
description:
"Garfield's Blackberry Blossom" is one of the great puzzles of the old-time fiddle canon — a tune that exists in the shadow of a more famous melody sharing its name. To call this the "older" Blackberry Blossom is not quite right; it is simply a different tune altogether. When bluegrass fiddler Arthur Smith recorded "Blackberry Blossom" in the 1930s, he created something so influential it eventually swallowed the older melody's identity. The prefix "Garfield's" — possibly coined by John Hartford, who was meticulous about such distinctions — was retrofitted to preserve the older tune's separate existence.

  The melody belongs to northeastern Kentucky. Its primary keeper was Ed Haley (1885–1951), the legendary blind fiddler of Lawrence County whose playing was so singular that fiddlers across the region sought him out directly. Dick Burnett, himself a Kentucky fiddling institution, credited Haley as his source. Buddy Thomas, Snake Chapman, J.P. Fraley, and Ed Morrison — some of the most respected names in the northeastern Kentucky tradition — all carried versions of this tune.

  An origin story in Jean Thomas's "Ballad Makin' in the Mountains of Kentucky" connects the "Garfield" name to President James A. Garfield, assassinated in 1881, though the exact nature of that link remains debated. The two Blackberry Blossoms share almost no melodic similarity beyond a vague resemblance in their opening measures, suggesting they developed independently. A close companion tune is "Yew Piney Mountain." The notated version appears in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes (2011), p. 226.

  Sources: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), Jean Thomas "Ballad Makin' in the Mountains of Kentucky," Milliner-Koken Collection, community discussions, and fiddle music scholarship.

title: Garfield's March
description:
GARFIELD'S MARCH. AKA - "Garfield's Funeral March." Old-Time. The piece was derived from a piece of sheet music called "Garfield's Funeral March," dating from the 1881 assassination of President James A. Garfield [1] (Wolfe, 1997), however, there were a number of pieces with the same name (by Edwin Christie, E. Gilmore and others), mostly minor-key dirges. The tune was recorded in Ashland, Kentucky, by Kanawha County, West Virginia, fiddler Clark Kessinger (1896-1975) and his nephew Luches ("The Kessinger Brothers" as the record label denoted them) for Brunswick Records in February, 1928, learned from local W.Va. fiddler Abe Glenn in 1903 when Kessinger was aged seven 1.  The assassination of James Garfield

title: Gaston
description:
GASTON. American, Reel. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB. The melody is printed in George P. Knauff's Virginia Reels, volume IV (Baltimore, 1839, p. 3), published by George Willig. The tune is similar to "Nigger on the (?)reat" from an anonymous 1862 music manuscript collection (probably a fiddler's ms.), and the first strain is cognate with the minstrel tune "Hoop-de-doo-den-doo (2)." 

Source for notated version:

title: General Lee
description:
The tune "General Lee" (also known as "Dubuque") is documented from the playing of fiddler Vernon Riddle (1935–2011) of Spartanburg, South Carolina, recorded in the field in 1993 by Ashley Carder.

Riddle learned much of his style and repertory from Texas fiddlers while stationed in that state during his military service. This Texas influence is audible in the tune's character — it sits comfortably in the contest/breakdown style common to the South and Southwest.

The tune is documented as "pretty much true to the way" it was originally passed down from Vernon Riddle, with players learning it from him around 1984 at fiddle contests, often accompanying him on guitar.
Form: Reel (single/double time)
Origin region: United States — Southeastern / Texas-influenced tradition
Alternate title: "Dubuque" — suggesting possible older roots or a separate parallel tradition under that name
Classification: Listed in the Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org) as a US fiddle reel

title: George Booker
description:

title: Georgia Row
description:
GEORGIA ROW. AKA and see  "Walk Up Georgia Row," "Walking Down the Georgia Road," "Coon Dog (2)." Old-Time. USA, Northeastern Ky. A Major. AEae tuning (fiddle). The reel is similar to the well-known "Angeline the Baker." "Sammie Walker's Georgia Road" is a different tune with a similar title. A distanced version in the key of 'D' was repertoire of Russell County, Virginia, fiddler Uncle Charlie Osborne, albeit in the key of 'D' (the exact nature of the relationship of the two versions has yet to be determined). 

Buddy ThomasSource for notated version: Buddy Thomas (1934-1974, Emmerson, Ky.) [Milliner & Koken].

Printed sources: Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 232. 

Recorded sources: Heritage Records, Young Fogies II. Rounder 0032, Buddy Thomas (northeast Ky.) - "Kitty Puss: Old-Time Fiddle Music From Ky." (1976). Rounder Select, Buddy Thomas - "Kitty Puss: Old-Time Fiddle Music From Kentucky" (1998).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Getting George Bush Upstairs
description:
Perry RileyGETTING GEORGE BUSH UPSTAIRS. American, Reel (cut time). A Major. AEae tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'. The tune and title (of which there are several variations) long predate the American Presidents of that name. The source for most modern versions is Kentucky fiddler Perry Riley (1893-1986) who was an elder cousin to another famous Kentucky fiddler, Buddy Thomas.  Although lame from childhood, Riley was an itinerant laborer who wandered the South in search of work, living at different times in West Virginia and Arkansas1 As Thomas related to Mark Wilson:

There weren’t hardly any other fiddlers around when I was growing up, only Perry Riley and he’d just come through every once in a while. 

He’s my second cousin on my mother’s side. He worked in West Virginia and Arkansas a lot and he’d go away and nobody would even know whether 

he was dead or alive. Once when I was a boy, it was fifteen years before we ever saw him again2.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Getting Out of the Way of the Federals
Getting Upstairs
description:
GETTING UPSTAIRS [1]. English, Morris Dance Tune (2/2 time). G Major (Carlin, Mallinson): A Major (Bacon). Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'B (Sharp & Macilwaine), ABB, x4 (Mallinson): AABB (Carlin): AABA (Bacon–Hinton): AA'BA (Bacon–Headington). "Getting Upstairs [1]" is a tune from the villages of Headington, Oxfordshire, and Hinton, Northamptonshire, in England's Cotswolds (the Hinton tune was actually from Leominster, imported to Hinton where the dance was finally collected). It is an adaptation of the American blackface minstrel tune of the same name written in the 1830's by Joe Blackburn. Winston Wilkinson (Southern Folklore Quarterly, VI, 1, 1942, "Virginia Dance Tunes") suggests that the title derived from the Morris Processional Dance in which performers danced "down the street, into the village houses, up the stairs and down again." However, it seems clear that the title and tune were borrowed from American minstrel usage, particularly when the song lyrics are reviewed (as sung by the Headington Morris side):

Some likes coffee, some likes tea, 

Some likes a pretty girl, just like me;

Such a getting upstairs and a playing on the fiddle,

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Gilroy
description:
"Gilroy" is one of many alternate names for the tune more commonly known as "Gilderoy" (also rendered as "Guilderoy," "Gilder Roy," "Gilderoy's Reel," "Red Haired Boy," "Little Beggarman," "Black Rock," "Nellie on the Shore," "Old Soldier with a Wooden Leg," and others). It is classified as a Scottish/American reel.

The title "Gilderoy" is an Anglicized version of the Gaelic Gilleruadh or Giolla Ruadh, meaning "red-haired lad or youth."

Historically, Gilleruadh was the nickname of a famous Scottish highwayman named Patrick McGregor, who was captured and executed in 1636. The original song describes his exploits and moralizes on his fate.

title: Gilsaw
description:
GILSAW. AKA - "Gill Saw." Old-Time, Breakdown. USA, Missouri. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. "Gilsaw" was popularized by central Missouri fiddler Pete McMahan, and is on Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden's list of '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes'. There are some similarities to "Muddy Road to Texas." The origin of the tunes name is explored by Howard Marshall in his blog "Fiddling Missouri" [1], who followed leads provided by McMahan, who maintained that 'Gilsaw' was the name of an itinerant ("tramp") fiddler who played the tune while busking for change at the Wabash Railroad depot in Montgomery City, Mo. It was overheard by a fiddling sheriff, relates Marshall, by the name of Claude Gregory, an uncle of McMahan's, who learned it on the spot. Before he left the fiddler told Sheriff Gregory that it was "Gilsaw", but it was unclear whether he was replaying the name of the tune or his own name (Marshall points out that people with the name appear in the 1900 Missouri census in Callaway County, Mo.). Gregory taught the tune to a young McMahan, who remembered it with the prompting of friends, in his later years. 

Source for notated version: Fred Stoneking [Silberberg]; Pete McMahan (Bluffton, Missouri) [Milliner & Koken]. 

Printed sources: Milliner & Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 237. Silberberg (93 Fiddle Tunes I Didn't Learn at the Tractor Tavern), 2004; p. 15 (appears as "Gill Saw"). 

Recorded sources: Marimac 9059-CD, Lynn 'Chirps' Smith - "Midwestern Harvest" (1994). Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers Association 001, Pete McMahan - "Ozark Mountain Waltz" (1987). Voyager Records, Pete McMahon - "Now That's a Good Tune: Masters of Traditional Missouri Fiddling." Yodel-084, Rhys Jones - "I Got a Bull Dog."

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Glory at the Meeting House
description:
| Attribute | Details |
|---|---|
| Full Name | Glory in the Meeting House (also "Glory at the Meeting House") |
| Origin | Eastern Kentucky, USA |
| Mode/Key | E Modal / E Dorian (sometimes D Dorian or D minor in other versions) |
| Special Tuning | EDAE (G string tuned down to E) |
| Structure | Multi-part reel; some versions "crooked" (irregular phrasing) |
| First Recorded | 1937, Library of Congress |

The key-of-E fiddle tune "Glory in the Meeting House" comes from Kentucky fiddler Luther Strong, who recorded it in 1937. The recording is attributed to Luther Strong, in E Modal tuning (EDAE), and was recorded for Music of Kentucky Vol. 2 (Yazoo 2014), captured by Alan and Elizabeth Lomax on October 18, 1937.

Strong's version is in the key of E minor and is played with the G string tuned down to E, making the fiddle tuning E-D-A-E. He recorded his version for Alan Lomax and the Library of Congress in 1937.

Luther Strong (1892–1962) was from Perry County, eastern Kentucky — a region with an exceptionally rich fiddling tradition.

title: Going Across The Prairie
description:
"Going Across the Prairie" is closely associated with Cleo Persinger, a Missouri fiddler. On the old-time fiddler's tune lists, the word prairie is notably scarce — perhaps limited to just one or two examples — and Persinger's tune stands as the prime example.

Persinger came from a deep fiddling family: both his father and his great-grandfather were fiddlers, and his great-great-grandfather once played the violin at concerts.

He began fiddling at age 15 and entered his first contest at 19 — one of the three in which he won no prize. In his second contest he placed sixth, and won first place in his third.

Like most country fiddlers of his era, Persinger could not read music; he learned his tunes by listening to others, to the radio, and to the phonograph. He recalled his only formal music lessons, given to him at age 18 by an old itinerant music teacher — which ended abruptly.

title: Going Down To Cairo
description:
"Going Down to Cairo" is a fiddle tune and play party song that has distinct echoes of frontier Illinois. It is also known as "Black Them Boots," "Cairo," and "Goodbye Liza Jane." It is a version of "Liza Jane," often used for play-party games and dances.

Cairo is a river town on the Mississippi at the mouth of the Ohio — an important river port due to its location at the confluence of the two rivers. It had the reputation as a somewhat lurid attraction to the river traffic. The town name "Cairo" is locally pronounced "Kay-row."

It's one of "a handful of folk songs native to the state of Illinois," according to Chicago's Old Town School of Folk Music. In his book Folk Songs and Singing Games of the Illinois Ozarks, David McIntosh said it comes from a "play party" circle dance for eight couples. In spite of its strong association with children's singing games, it traces back to Cairo's past as a wide-open river town when farmers shipped corn to market there by flatboat.

According to McIntosh's source for the song, "It was pretty hard to find a good place to pass the time away so they began going to the saloons and various other places where they were entertained." The women noticed on the return trips that the men "blacked their boots" and dressed up a great deal more than usual and began to make frequent trips to Cairo.

title: Going Down the River
description:
GOING DOWN THE RIVER. AKA - "Going up the River," "Pretty Girl Going Down the River." AKA and see "Boating Up Sandy (4)," "Sandy River" (Western N.C. title), "Little Dog Trottin' Down The River," "Little Dutch Girl (1)" (Ozarks title), "Sailing Down the River," "Davy Davy." American, Reel (cut time). USA; Kentucky, N.C., Missouri. F Major (Dr. Smith's): A Major (Fraley). Standard or AEae tuning (J.P. Fraley) (fiddle). AABB.  "Going Down the River" was recorded for Victor Records in Memphis, Tenn., in September 1928 by the Arkansas group Dr. Smith's Champion Hoss Hair Pullers, although it was not released by Victor until 1929. It featured the twin fiddling of Brian Lackey and Clark Duncan on the cut. However, the a very similar version had been recorded a year earlier by The Hill Billies (Tony Alderman & Charlie Bowman, fiddles) as "Boating Up Sandy (4)," one of many different tunes by that title.  The following words were associated with the tune by Kentucky fiddler J.P. Fraley:

Oh, my little girl, if you don't do better,

Put you on a boat, gonna send you down the river.

Boat began to sink, my heart began to quiver,

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Going To The Free State
description:
This is a lively two-part fiddle tune in cross A tuning (AEae) from northeast Virginia fiddler John Ashby (1915–1979).

Ashby began playing fiddle in 1926 at his home near Warrenton, Virginia. He was influenced by his Uncle Joe, local postmaster John Sullivan, and neighbors Walt Graham, Cy Kines, and John Sinclair — learning tunes such as "Hornpipe in A" and "Rattlesnake Bit the Baby." Circa 1940, John formed the Free State Ramblers, a band consisting of family and musician friends.

Ashby was known as a long bow fiddler, and his band, the Free State Ramblers, hailed from Fauquier County, Virginia.

title: Going To Town
description:
"Going to Town" comes from the great Arthur Smith, who was one of the innovators on the Grand Ole Opry in the 1930s and very influential on old-time and bluegrass fiddlers and all who heard him.

"Going to Town" is Arthur Smith's version of "Katy Hill," recorded in August 1937 in Charlotte, N.C., by Arthur Smith (fiddle), Alton Delmore (guitar), and Rabon Delmore (guitar) — performing together as the Arthur Smith Trio.

It was released on Bluebird B-8101 by the Arthur Smith Trio (1937). It has since been reissued on several compilations, including County Records CO-CD-3526, Fiddlin' Arthur Smith & His Dixieliners (2002).

title: Going Uptown
description:
John Hartford's note, given alongside his transcription of the tune, reads: "Oscar Stone added this part to 'Ragtime Annie (1)' (which it sounds like in the 'A' part) so, according to Howdy [Forrester, Nashville fiddler], he could claim it."

In other words, the tune was essentially born from a creative embellishment of "Ragtime Annie." Fiddler Dan Levenson notes that "Going Uptown" comes from the playing of Howdy Forrester, recorded on Home Made Sugar And a Puncheon Floor (Howdy and John Hartford), where Howdy talks about another fiddler — perhaps Tommy Jackson — coming up with it by possibly mis-remembering "Ragtime Annie."

| Person | Role |
|---|---|
| Oscar Stone | Tennessee fiddler; credited with originating the tune by adding a new part to "Ragtime Annie" |
| Howdy Forrester | Nashville fiddler; passed the tune along and is the main oral source for its story |
| Tommy Jackson | Possibly the one who actually "mis-remembered" Ragtime Annie into Going Uptown (per Howdy's account) |
| John Hartford | Transcribed the tune and documented the story in Devil's Box (1988) |

title: Going to the Wedding to Get Some Cake
Golden Ticket
description:
"The Golden Ticket" is a beautiful creation of fiddler Eric Merrill that has become a jam favorite in many corners of the old-time scene. It was released on October 4, 2004, on his album The Western Star.

The composer credit is well-documented: as Adrienne Young noted in the liner notes to her album Art of Virtue, "This song was written by our fiddle player, Eric Merrill. It is from his record The Western Star."

The Golden Ticket is "perhaps a bit elusive in its melodic and even harmonic structure, with a brief appearance of a D chord to open the tune." It is catalogued in the Traditional Tune Archive as a reel in the key of G, in standard tuning (GDAE).

The tune's path through the folk community is a classic example of oral transmission:
Roger Netherton got it from an amateur recording of Rhys Jones playing it at a contra dance. A local friend who gave the recording noted that Rhys used to play it a lot, though it doesn't appear on any of Rhys's CDs.
The impression was that it was a modern old-time-style tune, but that Rhys hadn't written it.
At the Winfield festival in 2011, Roger was in the fiddle contest finals with Tricia backing him on guitar. As they were about to walk onstage, Roger spontaneously asked if she knew "Golden Ticket." She replied, "Yeah, that's a sweet tune" — and they played it on stage without any preparation.

title: Gold Rush
description:
GOLD RUSH. American, Reel (whole time). A Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB'. Composed by legendary bluegrass mandolin player wikipedia:Bill Monroe and his band's fiddler at the time, Byron Berline (The late Monroe had over 63 fiddlers in his group at various times), around 1967. It is only Monroe's name on the credits, however. After graduating college, Berline played with Monroe for about seven months before being drafted into the US army. "Gold Rush" was recorded by Mike Yates in 1980 from the playing of fiddler Pug Allen of Stuarts Draft, Augusta County, Va. At the time Allen was adamant that he knew the tune years before Monroe's recording was issued. Dave Barton relays that Missouri fiddler Fred Stoneking maintains the tune was modeled after a local tune called "Burt County Breakdown," and suspects that Berline (who is from Oklahoma) may have reworked an older tune he heard. The "Burt County" title and tune was sourced to Burt County, Nebraska, fiddler Bob Walters (by Howard Marshall), however, and the breadth of its dissemination is unknown.

Recorded sources: - Caney Mountain Records CLP 228, Lonnie Robertson (Mo.), c. 1971-72. County 2705, Kenny Baker - "Master Fiddler." Musical Traditions MTCD321-2, Pug Allen (et al) - "Far in the Mountains" (2002). Philo 1023, "Jay & Lyn: Songs, Ballads & Fiddle Tunes" (1975). RSS MLP-538, LP, Pete McMahan - "Missouri Fiddlin' No. 2" (198?). Voyager 340, Jim Herd - "Old Time Ozark Fiddling."

See also listing at: 

 Jane Keefer's Folk Music Index: An Index to Recorded Sources [1]

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Goodbye Girls
description:
"Goodbye Girls, I'm Going to Boston" is an American reel in cut time, with the 'A' part in A Major and the 'B' part in A Mixolydian, typically played in AEAE cross-tuning on the fiddle. It is rooted in the Appalachian tradition and functioned as a "play party game/dance," popular in early education in North America.

According to its listing in Cecil Sharp's English Folk Songs of the Southern Appalachians, it was collected from a "Mr. Hillard Smith at Hindman, Knott County, KY, Sept. 20, 1917." Hindman is Art Stamper's hometown.

A song by this title is also associated with Jean Ritchie, whose version is nearly identical to the one collected by Cecil Sharp and Maud Karpeles in Hindman, eastern Kentucky, around 1917.

The tune runs deep in the Stamper family of Hindman, Kentucky:
Art Stamper's father, Hiram Stamper of Hindman, Kentucky, had a version of the tune, albeit a "crooked" one different from his son's.
Art learned it from his father, Hiram, who "also had a version of the tune, albeit a 'crooked' one different from his son's."
Art Stamper is considered one of the finest and most versatile bluegrass/old-timey fiddlers around — he helped anchor the Ralph Stanley band for years and is an outstanding performer.
Art recorded it on County CD2712 (The Lost Fiddler, c. 1982, taught to him by his father Hiram), and again on County CO-CD-2729, Goodbye Girls I'm Going to Boston (2000).
The tune was also performed by Charlie Stamper (Art Stamper's brother) at an impromptu jam session.

title: Goodbye Girls I'm Going To Boston
description:
"Goodbye Girls, I'm Going to Boston" is an American reel in cut time. It is set in A Major for the 'A' part and A Mixolydian for the 'B' part, and is typically played in AEae fiddle tuning. It is also known by alternate titles including "Going to Boston," "Off to Boston," and "Good-Bye Girls."

The tune's traceable American roots are firmly planted in Hindman, Knott County, eastern Kentucky.

According to its listing in Cecil Sharp's English Folk Songs of the Southern Appalachians, it was collected from a "Mr. Hillard Smith at Hindman, Knott County, KY, Sept 20, 1917."

A song by this title is also associated with Jean Ritchie, whose version is nearly identical to the one collected by Cecil Sharp and Maud Karpeles in Hindman, eastern Kentucky, around 1917.

title: Goodbye Liza
description:
Scholar Dan Gutstein traces the ultimate origins of "Liza Jane" songs to the name Liza Jane being "affixed to 'snotches' of folk melodies or as several 'one-verse songs' among enslaved people on plantations in several states" — which accounts for the many different titles, including "Little Liza Jane" and "Goodbye Liza Jane," as well as the wide variety of lyrics.

During the Civil War, some "Liza Jane" songs likely "leaked out" from the folk repertoire of enslaved people and were adopted by regiments from both sides of the war, including the 43rd United States Colored Troops Regiment, the 23rd North Carolina Regiment, and the Indiana 67th Regiment.

After the war, some "Liza Jane" variants were popularized in burnt cork minstrelsy — most notably an early version of "Goodbye Liza Jane," which was published as sheet music by bandleader Eddie Fox in 1871.

Drawing on those minstrelsy versions, Tin Pan Alley composer Harry Von Tilzer published sheet music in 1903 entitled "Goodbye, Eliza Jane," which became a "hit" through sheet music sales and cylinder recordings by the likes of Bob Roberts, Arthur Collins, and Billy Murray.

title: Granddad's Favorite
description:
"Granddad's Favorite" comes to us from West Virginia fiddler Ernie Carpenter, who learned it from his grandfather, "Squirrelly Bill" Carpenter.

Like many of the tunes in Ernie's repertoire, this was a family tune handed down from generation to generation, and the original name of the tune was lost after the older generation passed — so it simply came to be called "Granddad's favorite tune."

Ernie Carpenter is a member of a large West Virginia fiddling family, cousins to the Hammons, and descended from West Virginia's earliest settlers.

Ernie also wrote the tune "Elk River Blues", to commemorate the river in Braxton County that was the center of his family's life for generations, before the state built a dam that inundated the town where he was born and raised.

title: Grand Picnic
description:
GRAND PICNIC. American Reel. USA, Missouri. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. The tune is usually attributed to Joe Politte, a fiddler from the Old Mines, Washington County, area of Missouri, south of St. Louis. Politte was one of the few remaining fiddlers of his time who derived from the old French fiddling tradition from settlements along the mid-Mississippi valley. The tune has become a classic among Washington County fiddlers. It is on Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden's list of '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes'. Gordon McCann (2008) suggests the tune is of French origin and very old, perhaps from the old French settlers who formed communities in northern Missouri in the early 18th century.

Source for notated version: - Joe Politte, learned from Jules Boyer [Christeson, Phillips]; Ruthie Dornfeld (Seattle) [Songer]; Charlie Pashia (1909–1994, Old Mines, Missouri) [Beisswenger & McCann].

Printed sources: -  Beisswenger & McCann (Ozarks Fiddle Music), 2008; p. 107.

Christeson (Old Time Fiddler's Repertory, vol. 2), 1984; p. 62.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Great Big Taters
description:
The melody is directly related to "Sail Away Ladies" (and thus to "Sally Ann"), and some indicate it is merely a variant of that tune, though the title "Great Big Taters" and its variations is considerably disseminated in the South and Old Southwest.

Fiddlers in Arkansas and neighboring states call the tune "Great Big Taters in the Sandy Land" or "Sandy Land," while in other regions of the U.S. it is called "Sally Ann" or "Sail Away Ladies." It has also been linked to a song/tune primarily in the Midwest called "Hound Dawg Song" or "Every Time I Go to Town (the boys keep kicking my dog around)," published in 1912 — but likely much older, perhaps as early as the mid-19th century, according to Alan Lomax and Vance Randolph.

The tune goes by many alternate names, including "Big Sweet Taters in Sandy Land," "Sandyland," "Sandy Land," "Sandy Lot," "Better Quit Kickin My Dog Around," "Grease that Wooden Leg Sally Ann," and "Sail Away Ladies."

The tune is found across Oklahoma, Missouri, Arkansas, Texas, Alabama, and Mississippi. It's a deeply Southern and Old Southwest tune that traveled widely with settlers and fiddling families.

title: Green Fields Of America
description:
"Green Fields of America" (also written as Greenfields of America, and known in Irish as "Páircí Glasa Mheiriceá" or "Na Páircí Glais America") is one of the great transatlantic fiddle tunes — a melody that traveled with Irish emigrants across the ocean and took root deeply in both the Irish traditional and American old-time fiddle traditions.

The tune is generally thought to have Ulster origins, although at least one early version of the song has the emigrant bidding farewell to County Wicklow. It began life as an emigration ballad — a lament from someone leaving Ireland for the New World. As Paddy Moloney of the Chieftains put it, "it is surely one of the finest songs of emigration in our tradition and many versions of it abound."

The earliest published version is found in a 19th century collection by S.A. Such, London.

The melody itself has older antecedents. Breathnach (1963) says "Greenfields..." is similar to "Cossey's Jig," first published in Jackson's Celebrated Tunes (1774), a version of which appears as "Maid in the Meadow" and "Jimmy O'Brien's Jig," printed by O'Neill.

title: Green River March
description:
GREEN RIVER MARCH. American, (Slower) Reel. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. An archaic-sounding tune from the playing of fiddler Uncle Jimmy McCarroll of the Roane County Ramblers. McCarroll was born in 1892, in Wheat, Anderson County, Tennessee, and was still playing in the 1970's. McCarroll, who claimed Cherokee ancestry,  learned the tune from his grandmother, and family lore has it the tune originated on the Cherokee wikipedia:Trail_of_Tears.

Source for notated version: - Charlie Acuff (Union County, Tenn.), transcribed by John Hartford [Devil's Box].

Printed sources: -  Stephen F. Davis (Devil's Box), vol. 23, No. 3, Fall 1989; p. 29.

Recorded sources: - Columbia 15438-D (78 RPM), Roane County Ramblers (1929). County 403, "Roane County Ramblers" (east Tennessee. Originally recorded in 1929).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Green Willis
description:
GREEN WILLIS [1]. AKA and see "First Come in was a Bumble Bee," "Green Willis the Raw Recruit," "New Rigged Ship (1) (The)," "Old Hickory," "Noddin' Boy," "Raw Recruit (The)," "Chapel Hill Seranade," "Jackson's March." Old-Time, New England; Breakdown or Reel. USA, southwestern Va. D Major. ADae or Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. Green Willis was a 19th century fiddler from the Galax, Virginia, area whose name became associated with the tune, according to the Kimble family, who recorded the tune in 4/4 time. The melody, in 6/8 time, was also in the repertoire of Galax area fiddler Emmett Lundy (b. 1864), who recorded it when he was an elderly man. The melody had been employed as a “school breaking” march -- as Christian Wig explains: "the last day of the school year, a sad occasion for the children who would not see their friends for months. Nevertheless, there was a big celebration with “box lunches, speeches, dialogues (plays), music and perhaps a march. If a march were held, the children would line up behind the banjo and fiddle players and march out of the schoolhouse to the strains of this tune” and other marches like it" [Notes to "Lost Indian: Fiddle Tunes on the Frontier"]

A closely related, and probably ancestral tune (actually the same melody in jig version) is "New Rigged Ship (1) (The)," long popular with fiddlers and melodeon players in English traditional circles. It has been stated that a waltz setting is known as "Peekaboo Waltz (The)," however, the tune usually known by the latter title seems not to be related.  

Drinkin' moonshine at the age of fifteen,

Caused poor Willis' face to turn green;

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Grey Haired Dancing Girl
description:
The tune is attributed to Jumahl, a Maryland fiddler. Beyond this single attribution, the specific backstory of who Jumahl was, when the tune was composed, and the story behind its evocative title has not been widely documented in available public sources — a common situation in old-time music, where many tunes were passed down orally and their origins became obscured over generations.

"Grey Haired Dancing Girl" is played in the key of A, and is listed in The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes alongside its source recording: the Boiled Buzzards, from Old Time Music on the Air, Vol. 2.
Boiled Buzzards recorded "Grey Haired Dancing Girl" as a song on Spotify, dated 1994.
There is also a YouTube recording posted in 2017 by at least one other performer.

Most old-time fiddle tunes like this one are in the public domain and have no known authorship, though many have rich historical significance.

title: Grigsby's Hornpipe
description:
GRIGSBY'S HORNPIPE. American, Reel. USA, Texas. A Major. AEac# tuning (fiddle). From Texas fiddler Eck Robertson (1887-1975), who played it in a medley with "Rye Whiskey," recorded in March, 1963, at Robertson's home in Amarillo, Texas. Robertson said on record he was the only fiddler to play the tune.  The tune was perhaps named for “Grigsby’s Cowboys,” the 3rd Cavalry, a unit composed largely of cowhands from western states raised for service in the Spanish-American War by Melvin Grigsby, attorney general of South Dakota in 1898. Robertson biographer Chris Goertzen notes that Robertson was still a boy during the conflict at the end of the 19th century, and may have been quite taken with Grigsby's Cowboys. However, the war ended before the unit could be deployed and most remained in camp in Georgia, unfortunately where many succumbed to typhoid.

Source for notated version: - Clare Milliner & Walt Koken (Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 276.

Printed sources: -  County 202, "Eck Robertson: Famous Cowboy Fiddler" (1963). Rounder CD 0359, Skip Gorman - "Lonesome Prairie Love" (1996).

See also listing at:

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Grotts
description:
"Grotts" is an Illinois tune, played in the key of D in standard tuning. It belongs to the broader tradition of Midwestern old-time fiddling, particularly from the Illinois prairie and "Little Egypt" region (southern Illinois).

1. Stelle Elam
A version of the tune by Stelle Elam appears in the book Dear Old Illinois, which is a primary written source for Illinois old-time fiddle repertoire. Elam's transcription has helped preserve the tune in notation form.

2. Lynn "Chirps" Smith
Chirps Smith recorded a version of "Grotts" on his album Down in Little Egypt. Released July 15, 2003, Down in Little Egypt features Chirps Smith presenting tunes that evoke front-porch music-making on the Illinois prairie and dances in the hollers of Little Egypt, all in a style he calls simply "Midwestern." Smith is widely regarded as one of the Midwest's premier old-time fiddlers, and his recording of "Grotts" is one of the most well-known versions in the community.
Notation for "Grotts" is available in the Dear Old Illinois book.
The tune is in the key of D, standard tuning.

title: Grubb Springs
description:
In May of 1939, folk music collector Herbert Halpert recorded fiddler W.E. Claunch of Guntown, Mississippi playing a fiddle tune titled "Grub Springs" — named after a nearby community. More specifically, Grub Springs Branch is the name of a stream in Monroe County, northeast Mississippi, near the town of Caledonia. The tune name is almost certainly a piece of local place-name lore attached to the melody over time.

There are multiple distinct versions of this tune, associated with different fiddlers — and researchers emphasize they are not the same melody:

The most widely circulated version is classified as an Old-Time Breakdown in A Major, originating from Mississippi, recorded from W. Ernest Claunch by Herbert Halpert for the Library of Congress in 1939. The Mississippi Department of Archives and History later released it on the album "Great Big Yam Potatoes: Anglo-American Fiddle Music from Mississippi" (1985).

title: Gunboat
description:
"Gunboat" is a West Virginia breakdown with a title that tantalizes but refuses to explain itself. Gunboats were the great military innovation of the Civil War, and the name alone has led generations to assume this tune dates to that conflict — but there is no evidence to support it. What is certain is that the tune runs deep in the fiddle tradition of Braxton County, West Virginia, carried most prominently by Ernie Carpenter (1907–1997), an acclaimed fifth-generation fiddler who learned it from local fiddler Wallace Pritchard. Carpenter documented it on his landmark recording "Elk River Blues: Traditional Tunes From Braxton County, W.Va." (Augusta Heritage Records).

  The tune's identity is further complicated by its constellation of alternate names. Melvin Wine, the great Braxton County contemporary of Carpenter's, called it "Gunboat Whistled into Georgi-o." It also appears as "Going Down to Georgie-o" and "Who'll Take Care of the Baby-O." The strangest alias is "Hornio" — which researcher Gerry Milnes traced in 1999 to "Horney Ewe," a Scottish dialect phrase that survived in the Appalachian mountains long after it was lost elsewhere. The same tune, then, carries both a Civil War industrial image and a vestige of Scottish pastoral life — a small window into how language and melody traveled and mutated across centuries.

  Played in AEae cross-tuning, the tune has an open, ringing quality characteristic of the central West Virginia style. The notated version comes from Kentucky fiddler Bruce Greene.

  Sources: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), Gerry Milnes research (1999), Augusta Heritage Records, community discussions, and fiddle music scholarship.

title: Half Irish
description:
"Half Irish" was composed by Owen "Snake" Chapman, a fiddler from Pike County, Kentucky. It was recorded on Rounder Records on the album Walnut Gap (Rounder CD 0418). Chapman composed the tune specifically to emulate the sounds of an Irish reel, and named it "Half Irish" to convey that intention.

The tune is written in 4/4 time and opens in D Mixolydian for two parts, then shifts into D Ionian for the third part, with a flattened C note in the penultimate bar as a flourish.

This modal shift gives the tune its distinctive half-Irish, half-American character — rooted in old-time Appalachian tradition while consciously mimicking Celtic sensibility.

The tune is actually Snake Chapman's interpretation of Bob Wills' song "Go Home With the Girls in the Morning." He almost always played it in standard tuning, but in the late '80s / early '90s, Bob Butler convinced him to try it in ADAD tuning for a cassette he produced. Later, on his Walnut Gap recording, Snake recorded it under the name "Half Irish" and returned to standard tuning.

title: Half Past Four
description:
HALF PAST FOUR. American, Reel (whole or cut time). USA; Kentucky, West Virginia. A Major. AEae tuning (fiddle). The same tune was recorded in the mid-20th century by Edden Hammonds (Pochontas County, West Virginia) who called it "Paddy on the Turnpike (1)." Paul Mitchell suggests that Henry Reed's "Granny" (on the Hollow Rock String Band LP) is a corrupt or undeveloped version of "Half Past Four." Braxton County, West Virginia, fiddler Wilson Douglas played the tune under the title "Paddy on the Pike."  See also the related "Same Time Today as it was Yesterday."

Printed sources: -  Clare Milliner & Walt Koken (The Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes), 2011; p. 280.

Recorded sources: - Copper Creek CCCD 0199, James Leva - "Memory Theatre." Rounder CD0421, Bruce Molsky - "Big Hoedown" (1997. Learned from a recording by Ed Haley, Ashland, Ky.). Rounder 1133, Ed Haley - "Grey Eagle, vol. 2" (1997). John Johnson - "Strange Creek Fiddling 1947" (the tune is mislabled as "Grey Eagle").

See also listing at:

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Hanging Around the Kitchen Until the Cook Comes Home
Harrington Valley Two Step
description:
Harrington Valley Two Step is a tune in the key of D, copyrighted by Calvin Vollrath (noted as "© Calvin Vollrath" in tune collections).

Calvin Vollrath is a well-known Canadian old-time and contest fiddler from Alberta, which suggests the tune likely has roots in the Canadian Prairie fiddle tradition rather than Appalachian old-time — though it has crossed over into the broader North American old-time fiddle community.

A widely circulated version of the tune comes from a Missouri fiddle workshop taught by Charlie Walden in January 2015, and an audio recording of that entire workshop is available on Charlie's website.

title: Happy Hollow
description:
HAPPY HOLLOW. AKA - "Happy Holler." American, Reel (cut time). A Major. AEac# tuning (fiddle). AA'BB. From fiddler Marcus Martin (1881-1974) of Ararat, near Swannanoa, western North Carolina, who was recorded playing the tune in 1942 by field recorder Artus Moser.

Printed sources: -  Susan Songer with Clyde Curley (Portland Collection vol. 3), 2015; p. 87.

Recorded sources: - CD2001, "The Rough Deal Stringband." Field Recorders Collective FRC 502, Marcus Martin - "Happy Hollow" (2004).

See also listing at:

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Hawks And Eagles
description:
The definitive source for "Hawks and Eagles" is Norman Edmonds and the Old Timers. Edmonds (1889–1976) was from Hillsville, in southwest Virginia.

Norman remained an active fiddler his entire life, recording his final album a few years before his death in 1976. He passed on his love of music to his family — several of his sons became musicians, one became a luthier, his granddaughter Barbara was recognized by the Blue Ridge National Heritage for her bass and dulcimer playing, and his grandson Jimmy won his first of many fiddle contest victories at the age of ten.

The tune was recorded by Norman Edmonds in 1973, released on Train on the Island (Spring Fed Records, SFR-DU 33002), in the key of D with ADAE tuning. It is referenced in the Milliner-Koken Collection of American Fiddle Tunes.

The Train on the Island LP featured Uncle Norm playing with his sons on guitars and Rufus Quesenberry playing no-nonsense clawhammer banjo.

title: Hell and Scissors
description:
HELL AND SCISSORS. Old-Time, Breakdown. USA; Arkansas, Kentucky. A Major. ADae tuning. A 'hell' is a leather holster used by tailors to hold a pair of scissors. 'Hell and Scissors' was also, in English slang, "an ejaculation of surprise and ridicule" (see Farmer, 1905). However, 'Hell and Scissors' perhaps referred to a region of terrain in Kentucky that was particularly difficult to traverse. For example, in the the early 1800's when neighboring Illinois was first being settled there were no roads or bridges, necessitating a slow and laborious journey by pioneer wagons. One three mile stretch between Big and Little Ocho rivers at Vandalia, was known as the "Hell and Scissors," which it took three days to cross [see "Portrait and Biographical Album of Morgan and Scott Counties, Illinois", 1889, entry for Stephen Holland Reid [1]).

The tune is in the repertoire of fiddler Bruce Greene, who learned it from Day's 78 RPM recording.  The title appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes and songs compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954. 

Source for notated version: 

Recorded sources: Library of Congress 1010B2, Jilson Setters {Kentucky fiddler J.W. "Blind Bill" Day} (recorded 1934 for John Lomax in Ashland Ky).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Hell Broke Loose in Georgia
description:
HELL BROKE LOOSE IN GEORGIA [1]. AKA and see "Hell Bound for Alabama," "Been to the East Been to the West," "Great Big Yam Potatoes." American, Reel. C Major ('A', 'B' and 'D' parts) & A Minor ('C' part). Standard tuning (fiddle). AABCC'DD'. The title perhaps dates to the gold rush in Georgia before the settlement of Gordon County in 1850 (approx. c. 1830). There are three distinct fiddle tunes that have been identified with this title. The tune was used in 1899 in a Gallatin Tenn. fiddle contest as a category tune - each fiddler played a version, with the best version winning a prize (all fiddlers playing a rendition of the same commonly known tune was formerly a common way of structuring fiddle contests) [C.Wolfe, The Devil's Box, vol. 14, No.4, 12/1/80]. Cauthen (1990) finds reference to a Georgia fiddler, Ben Smith, who served with the 12th Alabama Infantry in the Civil War, and was known to have played the tune in that conflict. She also cites A.B. Moore in his History of Alabama (1934) who said it was one of the standard tunes in the square dance fiddler's repertoire. The melody "Streak o' Lean Streak o' Fat" is related to Phillips' version of the tune, as is "Big Footed Nigger (2)" and "Possum up a Gum Stump (2)." This was the four-part version recorded by the Skillet Lickers. The title appears in a list of traditional Ozarks Mountains fiddle tunes compiled by musicologist/folklorist Vance Randolph, published in 1954.

Source for notated version: - Ruthie Dornfeld (Seattle) [Phillips].

Printed sources: -  Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 110. Songer (Portland Collection), 1997; p. 94.

Recorded sources: - County 526, "The Skillet Lickers, vol. 2" (1975). Heritage 048, Lowe Stokes - "Georgia Fiddle Bands" (Brandywine, 1982).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Hell on the Potomac
description:
HELL ON THE POTOMAC [1]. AKA and see "Hell on the Wabash (1)," "Wake Up Susan (1)," "Hell on the Rappahannock," American, Reel. USA, southwestern Pa. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AB. Bayard (1981) identifies this as "one of the three or four" tunes universally known by Pennsylvania folk musicians. The melody is usually known as "Wake Up Susan (1)" or "Hell on the Wabash (1)" and it is sometimes found with other parts; Bayard is not sure if this means the tunes with different titles are "divergently evolving cognate tunes" or the result of trading strains or "otherwise infecting one another." Ultimately, the first strain is derived from the tune whose most famous title is "Mason's Apron." The "Hell on the (insert place-name)" is a floating title, and a popular naming convention, and were attached to a variety of different melodies at the whim of a fiddler.  Other tunes using more-or-less similar melodic material are "Night We Made the Match (The)," "Picnic Romp," "Jack of Diamonds (1)" (Thede), "Cottage by the Sea (The)," "Red-Headed Girl (The)." 

Source for notated version: versions by 17 southwestern Pa. fifers and fiddlers [Bayard]. 

Printed sources: Bayard (Dance to the Fiddle), 1981; No. 352A-Q, pp. 346-353.

Back to Hell on the Potomac (1)

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Hell Up Coal Holler
description:
HELL UP COAL HOLLER [1]. AKA - "Hell Up Coal Creek Holler." American, Reel (cut or 2/4 time). USA, West Virginia, southwest Virginia. C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB (Reed): AA'BB' (Milnes). Gerry Milnes and Henry Reed's versions are similar, albeit with parts reversed. A different tune by this name is said to have been in eastern Kentucky fiddler Ed Haley's [1] (1885-1951) repertoire.  

Source for notated version: -Armin Barnett [Phillips].

Printed sources: - Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 1), 1994; p. 110.

Recorded sources:   -"Old Tyme Fiddling/Old Time Way." Jim Martin Productions JMP201, Gerry Milnes (et al) - "Gandydancer." Shanachie Records, Gerry Milnes & Lorraine Lee - "Hell Up Coal Holler" (1999).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Henry King's Reel
description:
"Henry King's Reel" is a fiddle tune written by Trevor Stuart of Haywood County, North Carolina. It is a modern old-time composition — not an ancient anonymous traditional tune — but it has been embraced widely across the old-time music community.

The tune's origin story comes directly from Trevor Stuart himself. He composed it and named it after their great-grandfather, Henry King, born 1856, who was a fiddler, Methodist preacher, mortician, and barber among other things. His grandmother, Myrtle King Stuart, told him many stories about Henry King — including how he'd cut every dead man's hair in Sandy Mush. The stories about Henry King staying up all night and playing for dances inspired Trevor to play fiddle, and as soon as he had a few tunes, he'd play for her and watch the excitement in her eyes.

This is a rare case in old-time music where we know exactly who composed a tune, who it was named for, and why — a deeply personal tribute connecting generations.

Trevor and Travis Stuart learned to play old-time mountain music from members of their community in Haywood County, North Carolina and surrounding counties, including Byard Ray, the Smathers Family, and North Carolina Folk Heritage Award recipient Red Wilson. Trevor passed away in 2016. Travis Stuart is available to play for concerts, festivals, dances, and to teach workshops.

title: Henry Reed's Breakdown
description:
HENRY REED'S BREAKDOWN. AKA - "Breakdown in 'A'," "Reed's Reel." American, Reel (whole time). A Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AA'BB'CC'. This unnamed reel was in the repertory of fiddler Henry Reed (1884-1968) of Glen Lyn, Giles County, southwest Virginia, who was recorded at his home by Alan Jabbour for the Library of Congress. Jabbour thought it was related to bluegrass musician Ralph Stanley's "Clinch Mountain Backstep".  Reed himself, while not remembering the name, opined that it was "as old as the mountains." Compare also with "Pretty Little Cat," which, while a different tune, has similar melodic and harmonic content.

Recorded sources: - Library of Congress AFS 13703B24, Henry Reed (1967).

See also listing at: 

 Hear Henry Reed's 1967 field recording by Alan Jabbour at the Library of Congress [1]

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Highlander's Farewell
description:
"Highlander's Farewell" is considered one of the most unique and interesting tunes from renowned Galax, VA fiddler Emmett Lundy (1864–1953). It is fortunate that Alan and Elizabeth Lomax recorded him in 1941 at the Galax Fiddlers' Convention, including an interview. That field recording — made by the Lomaxes for the Library of Congress — is the primary source for the tune as we know it in old-time music today.

Lundy indicated he had the tune from his mentor, fiddler Green Leonard. Many of Lundy's tunes came from "ol' man Greenberry Leonard" (1810–1892) — the brag fiddler of the region who was never recorded. So the tune passed through an unrecorded 19th-century Appalachian fiddler before reaching Lundy, whose version was fortunately preserved.

On the Library of Congress recording, Lundy recounts the traditional story associated with the tune — at least as it was known in Virginia. On the recording, Lundy explains: "This piece was composed in the old country, where they had war in Scotland. And when the Highlanders took their departure from the Lowlands. A Highlander had a sweetheart in the Lowlands, and they just give him so long for to bid her farewell; and the low part of this represents the man and the high part, the lady."

This dramatic two-voice structure — low octave = the man, high octave = the woman — is one of the tune's most striking musical features and makes it unlike almost any other piece in the old-time canon.

title: High Yellow
description:
HIGH YELLOW. Old-Time, Breakdown. USA, western Virginia. C Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. The title was a term applied to a mulatto or light-skinned African-American. The tune is sourced to Glen Lynn, southwest Virginia, fiddler Henry Reed (1884-1968), who was visited by folklorist Alan Jabbour in 1966-67 and who collected a wealth of tunes and lore from him. According to Alan Jabbour, this rag-time influenced tune was learned by Reed from a Black fiddler by the name of Mr. Hites(?), who lived in Pennsylvania. However, Jabbour also states (on the LOC American Memory "Fiddle Tunes of the Old Frontier site [1]) in his notes that Reed told him he learned the tune from a mulatto fiddler from Texas, and on another occasion Reed suggested that this fiddler was from Cabell County, West Virginia. Reed had no title for the tune; the one given above was supplied by Jabbour and his former band-mates in the Hollow Rock String Band.  

Source for notated version: Woody Woodring [Phillips].

Printed sources: Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes), vol. 1, 1994; p. 112.

Recorded sources: Flying Fish FF-055, The Red Clay Ramblers - "Merchants Lunch" (1977. Credited to Henry Reed). CD, Alan Jabbour, James Reed, Bertram Levy - "A Henry Reed Reunion" (2002).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Hob Dye
description:
1. The folk-legend version: The lore attached to the tune has it that it was composed after one Hobb Dye, who was a bootlegger from Texas who ended up incarcerated. A YouTube comment also says the tune is named after a Texas fiddler named Hobson Dye.

2. The machine-trade theory: Hobs and dies are terms from the machine trade (i.e., "gear hobber"), although the lore attached to the tune has it that the tune was composed after one Hobb Dye, who was a bootlegger from Texas.

3. Alternate title speculation: Some have speculated that it was originally entitled "Hob Died."

The title is often spelled "Hob Dye," and less often "Hob(b) Die."

title: Hogeyed Man
description:
"Hog-Eyed Man" (also spelled "Hog Eye Man," "Hogeyed Man") is one of the most fascinating tunes in the old-time American fiddle repertoire — a piece with tangled roots spanning sea shanties, African American work songs, minstrel stages, Appalachian hollows, and even trans-Atlantic folk exchange with Ireland.

It is widely believed the tune started life as a Negro work song, possibly among railroad laborers in the United States. Folklorist Stan Hugill traces its history from navvies to river boat sailors on the Mississippi and Missouri rivers, to cotton workers in the Gulf ports, and finally out onto the deep-water vessels.

A "hog-eye" was apparently a type of barge used in the canals and rivers of America from the 1850s onward, which likely gave the "Hog-Eyed Man" his name — a type of laborer, navvy, or roustabout, usually depicted in songs as a man of African American origins, who found himself in a romantic situation with an unchaste woman named Sally or Sally Jane.

Whall dates the shanty to 1849/1850 and points out that "until the roads were made, there was great business carried on by water, the chief vehicles being barges called 'hog-eyes.'" The general consensus is that the shanty is of Negro origin, probably from river boatmen, and at sea it was used as a windlass/capstan shanty.

title: Hog Trough Reel (McMichen's)
description:
| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| Full Title | Hog Trough Reel |
| AKA | McMichen's Reel, McMitchen's Reel, Hog-Trough Reel |
| Form | American Reel (cut time) |
| Key | G Major |
| Structure | AABB' |
| Composer | Clayton McMichen (credited) |
| Tuning | Standard fiddle |

"Hog Trough Reel" was recorded for Gennett Records by Clayton McMichen's Georgia Wildcats in New York City in August 1932, and released on several subsidiary labels such as Crown, Melotone, Varsity, Beacon, and others. The composition is credited to McMichen, and was also recorded by Pat O'Daniel and The Hillbilly Boys, a Texas string band who recorded for Vocalion in the late 1930s.

The political trail of this tune is notable: In 1938, O'Daniel became a candidate for Governor of Texas and used the band in his campaign stumps. He was elected to that office, and later served as Senator from the state. Each of the band members received patronage jobs after his election, and O'Daniel kept them around to broadcast music from the steps of the Governor's mansion as they helped remind the public of his populist roots.

Clayton McMichen (January 26, 1900 – January 4, 1970) was an American fiddler and country musician. Born in Allatoona, Georgia, he learned to play the fiddle from his father and uncle. He moved to Atlanta with his family in 1913, working as an automobile mechanic. While there, he entered and won several competitions for fiddle.

title: Hollow Poplar 1
description:
"Hollow Poplar" is an Old-Time and Bluegrass breakdown. It is documented from Nebraska, Missouri, and Tennessee, and is played in G Major. It is also known under the alternate titles "Hollow Poplar Log" and "Old Hollow Poplar." The tune follows an AABB form.

The tune was popularized by Tennessee's Fiddlin' Arthur Smith. Smith was born in 1898 in Humphreys County, east Tennessee, and died in 1971.

Earnest Smith, the grandson of the famous Tennessee fiddler, told Susan Songer (1997) that this tune was his father's favorite and that it was the first tune Arthur Smith played on the Grand Ole Opry (WSM radio).

Although Smith had played the tune since the 1930s, he never recorded it until he made his "comeback" with the McGee Brothers in the late 1950s.

title: Home Town Band
description:
The tune is also known as "Old Town Band (2)" and "Centennial."

It is an American march in 2/4 time, rooted in southwestern Pennsylvania, played in G Major with standard fiddle tuning in an AABB (two-part, repeated) form.

The tune was "universally known to Pennsylvania fifers and some fiddlers," according to scholar Samuel Bayard (1981), who was not able to trace it back to British Isles antecedents — meaning it appears to be a distinctly American composition, likely originating in the Pennsylvania tradition rather than being transplanted from older European sources.

title: Hooker's Hornpipe
description:
HOOKER'S HORNPIPE [2]. American, Hornpipe or Reel (2/4 time). USA; north Missouri, Nebraska. G Major. Standard tuning (fiddle). AABB. The low part is reminiscent of Clayton McMichen's tune "McMichen's Reel." Hooker may refer to a fiddler, the Civil War general Joe Hooker, or, as Howard Marshall points out, to a laborer on a riverboat, a petty thief or pickpocket, a one-masted fishing boat, loggers, etc. "Hooker's Hornpipe [2]" is on Missouri fiddler Charlie Walden's list of '100 essential Missouri fiddle tunes'.

Source for notated version: - Bob Walters (Burt County, Nebraska) [Christeson]; Taylor McBaine [1] (1910-1994, central Mo.) [Phillips].

Printed sources: -  R.P. Christeson (Old Time Fiddlers' Repertory, vol. 1), 1973; p. 87. Phillips (Traditional American Fiddle Tunes, vol. 2), 1995; p. 201.

Recorded sources: - Missouri State Old Time Fiddlers Association 002, Taylor McBaine (b. 1910, Columbia, Mo.) - "Boone County Fiddler." Voyager 340, Jim Herd - "Old Time Ozark Fiddling." Voyager VRCD 344, Howard Marshall & John Williams - "Fiddling Missouri" (1999. Learned from Taylor McBaine and Jimmy Gilmore of Jefferson City).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Hop High Ladies
description: 'Hop High Ladies' is the American old-time descendant of 'Miss McLeod's Reel,' a Scottish reel that dates to the early 19th century or earlier. The primary melodic difference between the two is telling: the Scottish original ends phrases on the dominant (a harmonically open, questioning gesture), while the American version resolves to the tonic (settled, complete). This subtle shift transforms the feel of the tune from one of anticipation to one of satisfaction — fitting, perhaps, for the communal American dance tradition that adapted it. The tune's famous command — 'Hop high ladies, step lively too / Hop high ladies, the cake's all through' — connects it to the cakewalk tradition of Southern community dances, where the best dancers won a prize. Early recordings include versions by New England fiddlers, Appalachian string bands, and Midwestern dance orchestras, showing how thoroughly the tune permeated American folk music culture.
notes: D major with a light, skipping quality that matches the 'hopping' of the title. The American version should feel grounded and complete — land on the tonic. The Scottish Miss McLeod's version, if you know it, will feel different by comparison. Good for singalongs: 'Hop high ladies the cake's all through / Hop high ladies, step lively too.' In dance contexts, the caller can work with the clear four-bar phrases. Keep the tempo brisk but not rushed.

title: Hopping Rabbit (Saut du Lapin)
description:
"Saut de/du Lapin" translates as "Leap of the Rabbit" or "Rabbit's Jump." It's rendered variously in English as Bunny Hop, Hop of the Bunny, Rabbit's Leap, or The Jumping Rabbit. There is also a subtle French nuance: "de Lapin" vs. "du Lapin" — the "du" form would specify a particular rabbit, rather than the more general sense.

It is a French-Canadian reel, rooted in the rich Québécois fiddle tradition. Many French-Canadian tunes have origins in Scotland, Ireland, Wales, and England, brought to the Americas by early settlers.

There are actually two distinct tunes that carry the name "Saut du Lapin," documented separately in the Traditional Tune Archive:

The notated version traces back to French-Canadian violinist Joseph Bouchard (1905–1980), passed on via Québec button accordion player Philippe Bruneau, and subsequently transmitted to American fiddlers Ruthie Dornfeld (Seattle) and Lisa Ornstein.

title: The Horny Ewe
description:
"The Horny Ewe" (sometimes spelled Horney Ewe, and pronounced "Horny-O") is a tune by West Virginia fiddler Ernie Carpenter.

It appears consistently attributed to Carpenter across multiple old-time tune reference sources:
It is catalogued in the Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle resource directly under Ernie Carpenter's name.
It is also included in The Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes by John S. Lamancusa, again attributed to Ernie Carpenter, notated in the key of A.

The tune is short, rhythmic, and a little crooked — meaning it has an irregular or non-standard phrase length, a hallmark of certain West Virginia old-time fiddle styles.

title: Huckleberry Blues
description:
HUCKLEBERRY BLUES. AKA and see "East Tennessee Blues." Old-Time, Country Blues/Rag. D Major. Standard tuning (fiddle).

Dykes Magic City Trio

Source for notated version: 

Recorded sources: Old Homestead OHCS 191, "Dykes Magic City Trio" (eastern Tennessee) {originally recorded for Brunswick, 1927}.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz. Used under Creative Commons license.

title: Huntin' for the Buffalo
description:
"Hunting for the Buffalo" goes by several alternate titles including "Hunting the Buffalo" and "We're Gonna Hunt the Buffalo." It's classified as an American Reel (cut time), rooted in Arkansas. It is typically played in A Major, using either standard or the unusual BEgb fiddle tuning.

The most important name in the tune's traceable history is Jimmy Driftwood — a legendary Arkansas musician. Mike Seeger plays a version learned from singer, songwriter, and fiddler Jimmy Driftwood (1907–1998, born John Morris of Timbo, Arkansas), who had the tune from his two fiddler uncles who lived in Indian Territory for years.

Jimmy said he learned it from an uncle who was half-Cherokee and spent his early years living in the Indian Territory, but that he wasn't sure where the tune came from originally.

Mike Seeger first heard this tune from Ramona Jones, but didn't learn it until he heard a solo fiddle recording done by Jimmy Driftwood — the same musician who wrote "Tennessee Stud" and wrote the lyrics for "Battle of New Orleans," combining them with the fiddle tune "Eighth of January."

title: Hut In The Bog
description:
"Hut in the Bog" is a reel — a 4/4 time dance tune — rooted in the Irish traditional music tradition. There are actually two reels called "The Hut in the Bog," which causes some confusion in the folk music world. One of them is a traditional Irish reel with four known settings and has been added to over two hundred tunebooks.

The tune is supposedly a composition of Sligo fiddler Paddy Killoran, who called his version "On the Road to Lurgan" and recorded it on the Milestone at the Garden record, in Em.

However, the attribution is disputed. The tune is also known by the title "Killoran's Reel," but it is incorrectly claimed as a Paddy Killoran composition in some sources. The name "Hut in the Bog" itself may have come later — it's believed the tune was never called "The Hut in the Bog" until it was given that title — possibly mistakenly — on Mary Bergin's first solo recording.

title: Iberia Breakdown
description:
IBERIA BREAKDOWN. Old-Time, Breakdown. USA, Missouri. The source for this tune was biography:Bill Driver, an African-American fiddler from Iberia, Miller County, central Missouri, one of collector R.P. Christeson's sources in the mid-20th century.
